entry.title: TwinD: a deepfake detector that generalizes from face blending to fully synthesized faces
entry.summary: TwinD: Generalizing Deepfake Detection from Blending to Entire Face Synthesis arXiv · Nov 19, 2026Facial deepfake detectors are usually trained on blended fakes, which paste generated faces into real frames and leave blending traces. Newer generators synthesize whole faces without such traces, and prior detectors perform poorly on them. The paper proposes TwinD, trained on FaceForensics++ fakes plus two kinds of twins made from real frames, and reports a mean AUROC of 96.3%. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors propose TwinD, trained on reconstruction and blob twins without any generator, reporting 96.3% mean AUROC across 19 datasets, 8.9 points above the prior best.

entry.title: How feedback-free self-evolution changes agent skills: a systematic study
entry.summary: How Feedback-Free Self-Evolution Reshapes Agent Skills: A Systematic Study arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies what happens when models repeatedly rewrite expert-written agent skill documents without any tasks, run results, or judgments. Every model tested performed worse on every benchmark with the rewritten skills, dropping an average of 15 points on SkillsBench after thirty rounds. The authors propose SkillDiff, which marks expert knowledge in place without feedback or changing the skill text, raising SkillsBench pass rates by 4.8 points on average. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show feedback-free self-evolution degrades expert skills and propose SkillDiff, reporting a 4.8-point average gain on SkillsBench.

This establishes a uniform Markov property for these states. The authors build a classical representation using projective 2-designs, which yields a convergent cluster expansion with positive weights despite noncommutativity. entry.title: Quantum search for the minimum using numerical estimators with optimal query counts
entry.summary: Query-Optimal Quantum Minimum Finding from Numerical Estimators arXiv · Nov 20, 2026The paper proposes a quantum minimum-finding algorithm for objectives accessed through numerical estimators, avoiding the logarithmic overhead of amplifying estimate confidence before searching. At constant confidence, it finds a 2ε-optimal label using O(√N) base-estimator queries. The authors also give a result for preparations assigning known probability mass p to low objective values, with O(p^{-1/2}) queries. Applications include selecting near-optimal bounded expectations and guided ground-energy estimation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose quantum minimum finding avoiding logarithmic confidence amplification, claiming O(√N) queries and worst-case tight bounds for the additive error.

entry.title: Fast, in-place quantum algorithms for integer multiplication and inversion that need no ancilla qubits
entry.summary: Fast, in-place, and ancilla-free quantum algorithms for integer multiplication and inversion arXiv · Nov 20, 2026This paper presents quantum algorithms that perform integer multiplication, modular multiplication modulo a power of two, and modular inversion in place, overwriting the input with the output. These operations use O(n^{1+ε}) gates for any ε>0, with no ancilla qubits in most cases and only logarithmically many for one variant. The authors state these are the first quantum algorithms to achieve both subquadratic gate counts and sublinear ancilla counts for each of these in-place operations. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give the first in-place quantum multiplication and inversion with subquadratic gates and sublinear ancillas, unified under one theorem, mainly affecting quantum arithmetic theory.

entry.title: Stabilizing the Two-Photon Dicke Model Hamiltonian
entry.summary: Hamiltonian Stabilization of the Two-Photon Dicke Model arXiv · Nov 20, 2026This paper studies a model of N emitters coupled to light through collective two-photon interactions, which can make the energy spectrum unbounded and prevent a stable thermodynamic bright phase. The authors add a positive Kac-scaled number-Kerr interaction, which keeps the Hamiltonian bounded from below at all couplings while preserving its generalized Z4 symmetry. They derive the exact zero-temperature energy density and global phase diagram, and support the results with symmetry-resolved exact diagonalization up to N=128. ★★★★ Notable: The authors stabilize the two-photon Dicke model via a positive Kac-scaled Kerr term, giving an exact zero-temperature energy density and first-order phase diagram.

entry.title: Quantum error correction when noise is uneven and decoders have inaccurate information
entry.summary: When the Noise Gets Noisy: Quantum Error Correction with Disordered Noise and Misinformed Decoding arXiv · Nov 20, 2026This paper studies quantum error correction when noise varies across space and time and the decoder has incomplete or inaccurate knowledge of it, modeling physical error rates as random variables. The authors show that decoding performance is governed by the entropy and Bhattacharyya coefficients of the noise distribution. Numerical tests on surface codes agree with the theory across several noise settings. ★★★★ Notable: The authors model physical error rates as random variables, characterizing decoding performance via entropy and Bhattacharyya coefficients, with surface-code simulations reported to agree with theory.

entry.title: Joining quantum codes into quilts for logic without extra ancilla qubits
entry.summary: Stitching Quantum Codes into Quilts: Universal Logic with no Ancillary Qubits arXiv · Nov 20, 2026The paper introduces the "code quilt," a construction that directly measures a joint logical operator across two or more codeblocks without an ancillary system. The authors give explicit measurement circuits that need no physical qubits beyond those already used for idle syndrome extraction. The construction is based on a subsystem code, and several sufficient conditions are given under which code-capacity distance is preserved. Empirical analysis on bivariate bicycle and surface codes is reported, including decoding experiments comparing logical error rates to idle memory. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a code quilt construction measuring multi-codeblock logical operators without ancillas; the abstract reports experiments on bivariate bicycle and surface codes with decoding resu

entry.title: Non-contextual Pauli Hamiltonians are free fermions in disguise
entry.summary: All Non-Contextual Pauli Hamiltonians are Free-Fermion in Disguise arXiv · Nov 20, 2026This paper studies how to split quantum Hamiltonians into fragments that classical computers can handle, using non-contextual sets of Pauli operators. It shows that non-contextual Pauli Hamiltonians are free fermions in disguise and can be written with Majorana and Dirac fermion operators in a Jordan–Wigner-like encoding. Both central theorems are formalized in the Lean proof assistant. The authors also propose a heuristic algorithm for finding line-graph-based free-fermion fragments in molecular Hamiltonians. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show non-contextual Pauli Hamiltonians are free-fermion-disguised, give a Jordan-Wigner-like encoding, formalize theorems in Lean, and benchmark on molecular Hamiltonians.

entry.title: A new polynomial-style method for lower bounds on DQC1 query complexity
entry.summary: A sensitivity-constrained polynomial method for DQC1 query complexity arXiv · Nov 20, 2026This paper introduces a polynomial-style technique for proving lower bounds in the DQC1 quantum query model, based on a measure called sensitivity approximate degree for Boolean functions. It shows that every nonconstant total Boolean function on N inputs requires Ω(N) queries in DQC1, so DQC1 gives no asymptotic speedup for such functions. For symmetric partial functions, the paper characterizes this measure and derives tight quadratic separations from BQP query complexity. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce sensitivity approximate degree for DQC1 queries, report Ω(N) lower bounds for total functions, and tight quadratic separations from BQP.

entry.title: Classical complexity of quantum state transmission: the minimum classical communication cost of sending quantum states
entry.summary: The classical complexity of quantum state transmission arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper asks how hard it is to transmit quantum information using only classical communication. It defines classical communication models for quantum preparations and their minimum cost, called classical complexity. The authors prove this cost equals the classical communication needed to simulate quantum correlations in prepare-and-broadcast experiments, establishing a resource equivalence. They also characterise the classical complexity of noisy quantum states and present methods to certify it in quantum preparation devices. ★★★★ Notable: The authors define classical complexity of quantum state transmission, prove a resource equivalence with quantum correlations, and report exponential growth with quantum dimension.

entry.title: Precise experiment on s-polarized evanescent-wave reflection and the Casimir puzzle
entry.summary: Precise experimental investigation of the reflection properties caused by s-polarized evanescent waves and the Casimir puzzle arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The authors measured the amplitude and phase of low-frequency magnetic fields reflected from a metal plate, produced by an oscillating magnetic dipole. These quantities are determined entirely by transverse electric (s) polarized evanescent waves. The data disagree quantitatively and qualitatively with predictions using the standard Drude response function, which the authors say is excluded in this low-frequency region. The results are presented as clarifying causes of the Casimir puzzle. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors directly measure reflected low-frequency s-polarized evanescent magnetic fields and report that the Drude response is excluded, bearing on the Casimir puzzle.

entry.title: Entanglement-assisted quantum differential privacy: a framework against entanglement attacks
entry.summary: Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Differential Privacy arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper identifies an entanglement attack, in which an adversary sends one half of an entangled state to a quantum computer running a privacy mechanism, keeps the other half, and measures both jointly. The authors show this attack can fully break a mechanism that has a finite quantum differential privacy parameter. They propose entanglement-assisted quantum differential privacy (EA-QDP), characterize when a mechanism has a finite parameter, and show the optimal parameter can be computed by semidefinite programming. The depolarizing channel is recommended for bounding the extra leakage, and experiments on simulated and physical quantum hardware agree with the theory. ★★★★ Notable: The authors identify an entanglement attack, define EA-QDP, compute optimal parameters via SDP, and report validation on simulated and physical hardware.

entry.title: Algorithmic quantum sensing: using classical and quantum algorithms to measure time-varying fields
entry.summary: Algorithmic Quantum Sensing arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper presents a unified framework for measuring time-dependent fields using classical and quantum algorithms. It introduces three pulse-sequence protocols and quantum computational spectroscopy (QCS), which links quantum sensors to a quantum processor. The authors report that QCS surpasses the Heisenberg limit and keeps this advantage under certain noise conditions. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce quantum computational spectroscopy, reporting polynomial gains beyond the Heisenberg limit, with proofs of a fundamental separation from non-quantum-computational protocols.

entry.title: RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering
entry.summary: RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering arXiv · Nov 20, 2026This paper examines where the gains from reinforcement learning post-training of diffusion transformers come from. The authors add a fixed set of input-independent steering vectors to the block outputs of a frozen base model, with 65 times fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA on SD3.5-M. Fitted to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints without any reward, the vectors recover 90.0 to 96.3 percent of reward gains across six image models and 89.8 and 111.9 percent on two video models. Trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed weight-based RL on text rendering and human preference scores. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report that fixed, input-independent steering vectors recover 90-96% of RL post-training reward gains across several image and video diffusion models.

entry.title: Realized vs. population reliability: anytime-valid self-consistency certification under correlated reasoning
entry.summary: Realized versus Population Reliability: Anytime-Valid Self-Consistency Certification under Correlated Reasoning arXiv · Nov 20, 2026The paper studies a method for certifying language model self-consistency by repeatedly sampling answers and stopping once an anytime-valid e-process crosses a threshold. It argues that reasoning samples are positively correlated, so the usual independence assumption fails and the certified hypothesis changes from a realized null about a drawn belief to a population null about average model behavior. Experiments on GSM8K and AIME show that this distinction matters differently across tasks, and that a prompt-level procedure restores population validity. ★★★★ Notable: The authors separate realized and population nulls under correlation, show the single-unit e-process fails for population claims, and propose a prompt-level procedure tested on GSM8K and AIME.

entry.title: Represented but misread: how post-training changes reading out a model's internal representations
entry.summary: Represented but misread: Post-training changes how language models read out what they represent arXiv · Nov 20, 2026The paper compares linear probes with language models' own answers across six open-weight base models and their post-trained versions, analyzed with signal detection theory. Post-training lowered the sensitivity of the answers on average and changed how models use stated base rates. In a study of negated statements, post-training repaired cases where base models failed to use truth information their internal states already contained. ★★★★ Notable: The authors separate representation from readout and report that post-training changes readout rather than representation, testing six open models, checkpoints, model stitching, training experiments,

entry.title: An end-to-end quantum algorithm for solving a biomolecular simulation equation
entry.summary: End-to-End Quantum Algorithm for Differential Equations: Application to Simulating a Biomolecular System arXiv · Nov 20, 2026This paper presents an end-to-end quantum algorithm that takes classical inputs and returns classical outputs, targeting the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann (LPB) equation, a partial differential equation with variable coefficients used to simulate biomolecular systems. The authors implement every step, including state preparation, generating the quantum solution, and estimating system properties, and introduce a discrete representation for variable-coefficient PDEs on a grid. They report that the required circuit size scales polylogarithmically in the number of grid points and in the inverse accuracy, giving an exponential improvement in grid-point scaling over classical methods. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present an end-to-end quantum algorithm with a new discrete operator representation for variable-coefficient PDEs, reporting polylogarithmic scaling in grid size.

entry.title: Classical oracle separation of QMA from the QCMA hierarchy and quantum cryptography, even when P = QCMA
entry.summary: Classical Oracle Separation of QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy and Quantum Cryptography Even When P = QCMA arXiv · Nov 20, 2026The paper introduces a new problem called Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise (CHN) and proves, in the query complexity model, that it lies in QMA but is hard for the QCMA hierarchy (QCMAH). Using this problem, it constructs a classical oracle under which QMA is strictly more powerful than QCMAH. The paper also shows that, relative to an oracle where P = QCMA, various quantum cryptographic primitives, such as pseudorandom states with classical keys, can still exist. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce CHN, prove a classical-oracle separation of QMA from the QCMA hierarchy, and answer an open question of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal.

entry.title: GEOHunter: Tracing a Paid Promotion Network That Influences AI Search Answers
entry.summary: GEOHunter: Mapping a Generative Engine Optimization Network in the Wild arXiv · Nov 20, 2026This paper examines a network that sells visibility in AI-generated answers by publishing paid promotional articles on three major Chinese user-generated-content platforms. The authors identified 1,985 associated accounts and 466,357 inferred promotional placements spanning multiple months and product categories. Across nine generative engines from the US and China, 4.5% to 20% of retrievable cited pages were attributable to the network, and its clients were named in 52% of answers on eight engines. The authors conclude that content-level defenses are insufficient, and that account-level and platform-level signals are needed. ★★★★ Notable: The authors measure a paid GEO content network across three platforms, identifying 1,985 accounts and 466,357 placements and assessing impact on nine generative engines.

entry.title: Replicating AI Agent Security Incidents for Audit (ROGUE-AI)
entry.summary: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI) arXiv · Nov 20, 2026The paper presents ROGUE-AI, a multi-agent framework that rebuilds reported incidents involving LLM-based agents offline, paired with a control lacking only the blamed cause. Across 108 attempted replications, about 89% reproduced the reported harm. Most replications had no attacker, and agents missed ordinary hazards while doing their assigned tasks, causing more harm than prompt-injection replications. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors rebuild 108 real incidents with matched controls lacking the blamed cause, reporting 89% harm reproduction and 18% to 33% error rates across five models.

entry.title: Auditing LLM Intersectional Bias: Separating Interactions from Additive Effects
entry.summary: LLM GerryMandering: Separating Interactions from Additive Effects in LLM Audits arXiv · Nov 20, 2026This paper studies intersectional bias in language models, where people with several marginalised identities are treated differently than their separate identities would predict. It shows that a common audit criterion flags subgroups that independent single attributes already satisfy, producing many false positives on synthetic data. The authors propose ADDIS, which scores subgroups by their residual distance from an additive model and tests them against a Freedman-Lane null. Applying it to 13 open models on a synthetic Indian persona dataset, they find most flagged bias can arise from single-attribute effects, while a small set of interactions remains. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose ADDIS, separating interaction from additive effects via ARD scoring and a Freedman-Lane null, and report results on synthetic data and 13 open language models.

entry.title: What LLM agent sessions hold while waiting on serverless and agent runtimes
entry.summary: Held While Waiting: What LLM Agent Sessions Reserve on Serverless and Agent Runtimes arXiv · Nov 20, 2026This paper examines how LLM agents occupy computing resources while waiting for model replies. Using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore as its main example, it finds that each conversation reserves a separate isolated environment until the conversation is closed, so environments run out long before processing power does. The authors propose closing environments promptly after conversations end and sharing one environment among many conversations, noting that sharing requires platform support. Keeping conversations separate without reserving an environment for each waiting conversation is presented as an open problem. ★★★★ Notable: The authors identify that LLM agent sessions hold dedicated environments while waiting on the model, and propose closing and sharing fixes, evaluated via a simulation and a benchmark.

entry.title: Scaling classical hardware to make real-time quantum error correction both fast and accurate
entry.summary: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction arXiv · Nov 20, 2026The paper introduces Rapids, a streaming neural decoder co-designed with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) to be both fast and accurate for quantum error correction. For the distance-19 surface code, it decodes each syndrome round in under a microsecond on a single FPGA. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than existing real-time hardware decoders. The authors also show the design extends to other codes and scales across multiple FPGAs or custom silicon. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors co-design a neural decoder with an FPGA, reporting sub-microsecond decoding for the distance-19 surface code with a 240x lower logical error rate than existing real-time decoders.

entry.title: Statistical inference for neural network models with ill-conditioned random weights
entry.summary: Statistical Inference with Ill-Conditioned Random Weight Neural Network Sieves arXiv · Nov 20, 2026The paper studies random weight neural networks, where hidden-layer parameters are randomly generated and fixed, and only output coefficients are estimated. It shows that such random sieves cannot stay uniformly well-conditioned as their dimension grows, so the smallest eigenvalue of the population covariance matrix vanishes. The authors develop approximation, estimation, and inference theory that accounts for this ill-conditioning, and report numerical experiments on finite-sample behavior. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove random-feature covariance eigenvalues degrade with dimension and develop ridge-adjusted inference theory, validated by theory and numerical experiments.

entry.title: GateTrace: Where Crowd Crossings Are Missed Under Occlusion
entry.summary: GateTrace: Where Do Crowd Crossings Go Missing Under Occlusion? arXiv · Nov 20, 2026Pedestrian tracking is used to count people at event entrances and passageways, but totals do not show which crossings were missed. The paper introduces GateTrace, which derives reference crossings from annotations under fixed rules, matches system reports by person, direction, time and position, and traces where misses occur. On MOT20 development sequences, ByteTrack, OC-SORT and BoT-SORT recovered 38.9% to 46.7% of low-visibility reference crossings, compared with 98.1% to 99.0% at high visibility. ★★★★ Notable: The authors trace crowd-crossing misses by person, direction, time and position, comparing several trackers on MOT20 across two sequence groups.

entry.title: Classical algorithm for estimating ground energy of certain interacting fermion systems
entry.summary: Efficient Classical Algorithms for Ground Energy Estimation of Fermions with Conjugate-Pair Orbital Interactions arXiv · Nov 20, 2026This paper presents an efficient classical randomized algorithm for approximating the ground energy of fermionic Hamiltonians with conjugate hopping matrices and conjugate-paired orbital interactions, including attractive Hubbard models. The guarantee holds without assuming a physical spectral gap or weak coupling, and covers interactions beyond onsite density attractions. The method reduces ground-energy estimation to partition-function estimation, uses a discretization with controlled energy error to obtain a nonnegative weighted sum of squared determinant moduli, and applies the Chen–Liu log-concave counting theorem. The authors also obtain a sharper arithmetic bound by controlling the number of sampling runs and matrix updates and by using sparse matrices to reduce per-update cost. ★★★★ Notable: The authors reduce fermionic ground-energy estimation to partition-function estimation and apply the Chen–Liu log-concave counting theorem, reporting polynomial-time classical randomized guarantees fo

entry.title: Optimal Preemption for Keeping Information Fresh in Mean Age and Beyond
entry.summary: Optimal Preemption: Guaranteeing Information Freshness in Mean Age and Beyond arXiv · Nov 20, 2026This paper studies Age of Information (AoI), where an update in service must normally wait even when heavy-tailed delays raise its age. The authors propose a framework in which the sender can preempt an in-service update and sample a fresh one, for general service-time distributions and explicit action costs. Under nondecreasing age costs, a finite mean delay is shown to suffice for finite average age even with infinite delay variance. For exponential service the optimal rule uses constant thresholds, while for general delays the optimal preemption rule depends on both the age and the elapsed service time. ★★★★ Notable: The authors allow preempting in-service updates and reduce VaR and CVaR minimization to the same optimality equations, validated under Pareto and log-normal delays.

entry.title: OffBeat: multi-camera 4D capture with staggered firing beyond frame rate limits
entry.summary: OffBeat: Multicoset Sampling for 4D Capture Beyond the Camera Frame Rate arXiv · Nov 20, 2026The paper presents OffBeat, which treats a staggered multi-camera rig as a spatially distributed multicoset sampler and derives camera groups and firing order from calibration alone. Because each timestamp is recorded by one group, short-lived primitives are less likely to flicker in novel views. In simulated staggered capture on N3DV, OffBeat outperforms the full 4DSloMo pipeline with video diffusion in mean dynamic-region PSNR. Between the first and last synchronized frames, it also outperforms the best synchronized method of each scene. ★★★★ Notable: The authors model staggered camera rigs as spatially distributed multicoset samplers and derive a lifetime condition for flicker-free primitives. The abstract reports 3.04 dB higher dynamic-region PSN

entry.title: SKILL.PNG: Learning AI Agent Skills as Optimized Images
entry.summary: SKILL.PNG: Learning Agent Skills in Pixel Space arXiv · Nov 20, 2026AI agents are usually specialized with text-based skills, which cannot be optimized continuously. This paper introduces Skill.png, which represents a skill as an image whose pixels are optimized by gradient descent through the vision encoder of a frozen vision-language model. In 9 of 16 settings across 4 models and 4 benchmarks, it outperforms text skills optimized with frontier LLMs, using 64 to 256 image tokens instead of roughly 900 to 2000 text tokens. ★★★★ Notable: The authors optimize skills as image pixels via gradient descent through a frozen VLM encoder, reporting gains over textual skills in 9 of 16 settings.

entry.title: Sightline: Calibrated Data-Flow Summaries for LLM-Integrated Applications
entry.summary: Sightline: Calibrated Data-Flow Summaries for LLM-Integrated Applications arXiv · Nov 20, 2026This paper introduces Sightline, a tool that determines which input placeholders actually affect a large language model's output in programs that call LLMs. It reads a recorded call in one forward pass, learns from labels which attention reads count as uses, and calibrates pruning so only a chosen small fraction of true flows are missed. On 2,103 unseen repository families and four models, it outperformed seven closest methods and a hidden-state probe. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove placeholders flow to outputs only via attention reads and calibrate pruning from reads, reporting 1.6 to 2.6 times more spurious flows pruned than the best of seven baselines across

entry.title: NariQ: Sub-3-Bit Quantization for Long-Horizon Agent Tasks
entry.summary: NariQ: Sub-3-Bit Quantization for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper presents NariQ, a trellis-coded post-training quantization method that calibrates on tokens generated by the BF16 model in agent sessions rather than short web text. On Qwen3.8-27B, the 3.0 and 2.5 bits-per-weight versions match BF16 on DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, AIME, and RealWorldQA, while the 2.0 bits-per-weight version performs somewhat lower. The authors release the GGUF files and a llama.cpp fork for inference. ★★★★ Notable: The authors calibrate trellis quantization on BF16 agent-session tokens; they report parity with BF16 on DeepSWE and Terminal Bench at 2.5 and 3.0 bits.

entry.title: Front-running attack via causal overtaking in fair transaction ordering
entry.summary: Causal Overtaking in Fair Transaction Ordering arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies an attack on fair transaction ordering protocols, in which corrupted replicas observe a target transaction and submit identical signed copies of a responsive transaction through multiple client entries, so the response executes before its target. The authors formalize a class of receipt-order protocols, including Themis, and characterize the timing and network conditions under which the attack is feasible. They prove that receipt-only mechanisms cannot always preserve earlier-submission priority while preventing responsive overtaking. A mitigation is proposed and analyzed, and both the attack and the mitigation are evaluated through simulations using AWS and WonderProxy latency measurements. ★★★★ Notable: The authors identify causal overtaking across multiple client entries and prove receipt-only evidence cannot always preserve priority; simulations use AWS and WonderProxy latencies on Themis.

entry.title: Less Than Meets the Eye: Action-Set Identifiability and Principled Abstention for 3D Physical Geometry
entry.summary: Less Than Meets the Eye: Action-Set Identifiability and Principled Abstention for 3D Physical Geometry arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper studies whether bounded camera motions can distinguish competing explanations of the same image, such as a corridor, its mirror reflection, or a picture on a display. Intervene3D selects camera motions by maximin separability and answers only when available motions separate the remaining hypotheses, otherwise abstaining. On a synthetic benchmark, abstention removed all confident answers on unresolvable scenes, and an adequacy test lowered wrong answers on curved mirror scenes. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose maximin motion selection with abstention for 3D geometry ambiguity, reporting synthetic and real display experiments.

entry.title: The Delayed Societal Cost of Unfairness: How Decisions Reshape Populations So Fairer Policies Can Win Later
entry.summary: The Delayed Societal Cost of Unfairness arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper studies the societal costs of decision policies, covering both the decision-maker's loss and the unequal distribution of costs across demographic groups. It asks when a policy that is optimal on pre-deployment data can be beaten by a fairer policy once both are evaluated on the population each induces. Under Rawlsian and egalitarian fairness notions, the authors give conditions under which placing more weight on fairness lowers societal costs. They also find that when the decision-maker's loss is accuracy-based, post-deployment gains can come from declining qualification among decision subjects. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show that post-deployment population dynamics can make fairer policies reduce costs for both stakeholders, deriving conditions under Rawlsian and egalitarian fairness.

entry.title: Testing whether AI chat assistants catch distress signals spread across a conversation
entry.summary: Evaluating safeguarding in multi-turn conversations with AI assistants arXiv · Nov 19, 2026Researchers worked with three community mental health support workers to build nine scenarios involving cues of depression, psychosis, or domestic abuse. They compared whether six widely used AI models gave the same safeguarding responses when cues appeared together in one message or spread across a conversation. Across more than 7,400 conversations, most models met the support workers' standards far less often when cues were dispersed. The authors argue that safety evaluations focused on explicit signals may overstate how well safeguards protect people. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend safety testing to gradually disclosed multi-turn conversations, using support-worker gold standards across over 7,400 conversations and six models, reporting sharp drops when cues a

entry.title: Safe subgame resolving for multiplayer games
entry.summary: Safe Subgame Resolving in Multiplayer Games arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies how to refine a precomputed poker strategy in real time in multiplayer games with hidden information, where safety guarantees were previously missing. The authors prove the first conditional safety theorem for uncorrelated multiplayer subgame resolving, giving a post-hoc certificate that bounds how much the best-response gap can grow over the blueprint. Experiments on three-player Leduc and up to six-player Kuhn poker show the certificate flags every harmful update. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give the first conditional safety theorem for uncorrelated multiplayer subgame resolving, bounding the best-response gap by four terms; experiments on Leduc and Kuhn poker.

entry.title: How deep a language model settles on a word, and how long people read it
entry.summary: The Depth of a Prediction: Where Language Models Resolve a Word Predicts Human Reading Time arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper examines the layer at which language models settle on a word's prediction, a factor that relates to human reading time. The authors read each layer's prediction with the tuned lens and summarize the change in surprisal across layers as a resolution depth. On eight English eye-tracking and self-paced reading corpora and ten GPT-2, OPT and Pythia models, words resolved later, and the words after them, were read more slowly. Resolution depth improves held-out prediction beyond final-layer surprisal, entropy and the best single layer. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce resolution depth from layerwise tuned-lens surprisal and report it improves reading-time prediction over final-layer surprisal and entropy across eight corpora and ten models.

entry.title: When sounds turn heads: recovering event timing audio LLMs fail to state
entry.summary: When Sounds Turn Heads: Recovering Event Timing That Audio LLMs Fail to Say arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper finds that a few attention heads in audio LLMs track the queried sound, yet the model's final timestamps do not express what these heads track. The authors propose head-guided decoding, which needs no training, to rescore candidate timestamps using these heads while keeping the model's presence decision. The method improves timestamps for three audio LLMs across benchmarks, including recordings released after training. ★★★★ Notable: The authors find attention heads tracking queried sounds and use them for training-free timestamp rescoring, reporting mIoU gains on three audio LLMs and newer recordings.

entry.title: BlockJack: Cross-tenant redirection fault attacks on paged KV cache in LLM serving
entry.summary: BlockJack: Cross-Tenant Redirection Fault Attacks on Paged KV Cache Address Translation in LLM Serving arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper presents BlockJack, the first fault attack targeting KV cache address translation in LLM inference. By corrupting block-table entries in vLLM, it redirects one request's KV cache reads to blocks belonging to another tenant, without changing model weights, prompts, or cached states. The authors show across seven models that victim context can be exposed and responses can be steered, and demonstrate physical feasibility with Rowhammer. They also evaluate assignment validation as a defense. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report the first fault attack on paged KV cache address translation in LLM serving, where block-table corruption redirects reads across tenants. entry.title: Gradient boosting with Kolmogorov-Arnold units for interpretable regression beyond pairwise effects
entry.summary: Gradient Boosting with Kolmogorov-Arnold Units for Interpretable Regression beyond Pairwise Interactions arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper presents MJBoost, a gradient boosting method for tabular regression that uses a Kolmogorov-Arnold unit as its weak learner. The fitted model decomposes exactly into main effects, pair effects, and a higher-order remainder, allowing interpretation beyond pairwise interactions. On synthetic data and the OpenML-CTR23 regression benchmark, it achieves lower test error than the explainable boosting machine (EBM), and it is competitive with EBM and LightGBM on classification tasks. ★★★★ Notable: Uses Kolmogorov-Arnold units as weak learners to go beyond pairwise interactions in interpretable boosting; the authors report gains over EBM on synthetic and OpenML benchmarks.

entry.title: Self-orthogonal MDS codes from principal ideals
entry.summary: Self-Orthogonal MDS Principal-Ideal Codes arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies Euclidean self-orthogonality and the generalized Reed-Solomon (GRS) property for codes generated by a monic polynomial g and its shifts, with length r+k and dimension k, where 3≤k≤r. Over any algebraically closed field, the authors fully classify the generators that yield codes that are both self-orthogonal and GRS. For fixed r, k and characteristic, only finitely many such generators exist. When 3≤k<r, they show that each algebraically closed field supports infinitely many pairwise inequivalent, non-GRS self-orthogonal MDS codes. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a complete classification of self-orthogonal GRS generators over algebraically closed fields and prove infinitely many inequivalent non-GRS MDS codes, a strong theoretical result with

entry.title: Why Flat Drafts Stay Flat: Region-Mean Latents and Texture in Flow-Based Image Generation
entry.summary: Why Flat Drafts Stay Flat: Region-Mean Latents Govern Texture in Flow-Based Image Generation arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies why flat color-block drafts can keep a flat look in pretrained flow-based image generators even under photorealistic prompts. It finds that flattening photo regions shifts their regional means in VAE latent space, and experiments on FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image show that adding the photo-derived regional mean field restores texture. The authors also propose training-free rendering methods and draft-conditioned LoRA adaptation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a cross-scale mechanism linking latent regional means to texture in flow generators, validated via controlled field-exchange experiments on FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image.

entry.title: Closing Gaps in Temporal Fair Division of Chores
entry.summary: Closing Gaps in Temporal Fair Division for Chores arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies fairly dividing indivisible chores that must be assigned in a fixed order, with the full list known in advance but assignments irreversible. The authors show that for three or more agents, some instances admit no allocation satisfying temporal envy-freeness up to one chore (TEF1), even up to any finite factor, and that deciding TEF1 existence is NP-complete. They also show that minimizing social cost under TEF1 cannot be approximated in polynomial time, but for a fixed number of agents they give an FPTAS for the optimal temporal EF1 factor with social cost guarantees. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors resolve an open question, showing TEF1 allocations may not exist for three or more agents, with NP-completeness and social-cost inapproximability results.

entry.title: Full-rank and stable sampling for tanh neural networks
entry.summary: Full Rank and Stable Sampling of tanh Networks arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies recovering fixed-architecture feedforward tanh networks with P parameters from finitely many point evaluations. It characterizes the parameters where the realization map's differential has full rank and shows this set coincides with the regular parameters defined by Vlačić and Bölcskei (2021). The authors prove that almost every set of 2P+1 sampling points gives uniform-norm Lipschitz stability on compact subsets of this set, and that projected gradient descent and projected Gauss-Newton converge locally for exact observations. ★★★★ Notable: The authors characterize full-rank parameters as regular ones, prove 2P+1 generic samples give Lipschitz stability, and show local convergence of projected gradient and Gauss-Newton methods.

entry.title: Optimal impure quantum codes that recover erased qudits from few others
entry.summary: Optimal Impure (r,δ)-Quantum Locally Recoverable Codes with Explicit Minimum Localities arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies quantum locally recoverable codes, where erased qudits can be recovered by accessing only a small number of other qudits. The authors build CSS codes from nested pairs of generalized monomial-Cartesian codes. They obtain four infinite families of GKT-optimal impure (r,δ)-qLRCs with disjoint recovering sets, and determine their minimum localities. ★★★★ Notable: The authors characterize minimum localities of CSS codes via local relative distances and construct four GKT-optimal impure quantum LRC families with determined minimum localities.

entry.title: Signed but Unbound: The Gap Between What AI Payment Mandates Specify and What Crypto Wallets Enforce
entry.summary: Signed but Unbound: The Authority Gap Between Agent Commerce Mandates and Crypto Wallet Signatures arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper examines the gap between the payment terms an AI agent's commerce protocol specifies, such as merchant, order, amount, and facilitator, and the fields a token contract actually enforces through the wallet signature. The authors define nine constraint classes and derive them for 12 authorization configurations, including Coinbase's deployed Commerce Payments Protocol, with all 31,800 trials on local copies of deployed contract code matching the derivation. They introduce MandateLock, a minimal implementation that rejects all 10,800 modified mandates on deployed token code while accepting signatures from two independent signers. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors define an authority gap between agent payment mandates and wallet signatures, derive nine constraint classes, and report trials on deployed token contract copies plus sampled on-chain rede

entry.title: What anti-hallucination training actually achieves: saying less, cheap pruning, and the rest
entry.summary: What Does Anti-Hallucination Training Buy? Saying Less, Cheap Pruning, and the Rest arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper examines how much of the reduction in CHAIR scores from preference training for vision-language models comes from the model simply saying less, and how much a simple post-hoc probe can reproduce. It compares eight public methods on LLaVA-1.5-7B across several benchmarks, along with DPO checkpoints. It also measures how well DPO on the model's own samples labelled by the probe or a CLIP score recovers the gain of ground-truth-labelled DPO. ★★★★ Notable: The authors decompose hallucination reduction into saying less versus training gain, benchmarking against a frozen post-hoc probe across several models and benchmarks.

entry.title: How Reliable Are Language Model Explanations for Insider Threat Detection?
entry.summary: How Reliable Are Explanations of Language Models That Detect Insider Threats? arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper audits explanations from language-model detectors that flag insider threats in CERT's simulated workplace logs. It tests explanations by removing internal features and comparing the resulting score change against a similar control change. The authors introduce the tipping radius, which measures how sensitive the result is to the choice of distance metric. They report that explanations are fragile under this choice and that flag scores partly reflect who the worker is rather than what they did. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a tipping radius measuring explanation fragility to metric choice, auditing seven language models on CERT logs.

entry.title: Suppressing a hidden shortcut that limits gains from fine-tuning video language models
entry.summary: Suppressing the Shortcut Hidden Behind the Gains of VideoLLM Fine-Tuning arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies a shortcut in which Video Large Language Models learn to answer from textual patterns in their training data rather than from the video during supervised fine-tuning. The authors propose VETO, which projects the fine-tuning update onto the orthogonal complement of the subspace that text alone occupies in the base model's activations. Across seven VideoLLMs, VETO keeps the training-distribution gains of SFT, and on six benchmarks under distribution shift it outperforms SFT and relies more on the full input. ★★★★ Notable: The authors project SFT updates orthogonal to the text-only activation subspace, reporting gains across seven VideoLLMs and six shifted benchmarks.

entry.title: Uniqueness, proximity, and scaling in atomic splittable polymatroid congestion games
entry.summary: Uniqueness, Proximity, and Scaling in Atomic Splittable Polymatroid Congestion Games arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper presents a polynomial-time algorithm for computing exact equilibria in atomic splittable polymatroid congestion games with integral ranks and rational affine latencies. It first computes equilibria of integer-splittable versions of the game, then uses progressively finer packet sizes to recover the continuous equilibrium. The paper also proves that equilibria are unique for arbitrary real polymatroid ranks and convex, strictly increasing, continuously differentiable latencies. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a polynomial-time exact equilibrium algorithm for atomic splittable polymatroid congestion games and prove uniqueness for arbitrary real ranks.

entry.title: Distortion in Online Voting: how well sequential elections approximate ideal choices
entry.summary: Distortion in Online Voting arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies distortion in online voting, a framework combining computational social choice with online algorithms. Unlike offline elections where all candidates are known in advance, here a fixed set of voters is present from the start while candidates arrive one at a time. Each arrival requires an immediate, irrevocable decision to keep the current candidate or switch. The authors give upper and lower bounds for deterministic and randomized mechanisms under utilitarian and metric preference frameworks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce online distortion for voting, giving deterministic and randomized bounds under utilitarian and metric preference models.

entry.title: Measurable Does Not Imply Transportable: Checking Whether Model Explanations Hold in Future Field Trials
entry.summary: Measurable Does Not Imply Transportable: A Prospective Audit of Model Explanations in Multi-Year Field Trials arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper examines whether explanations of machine learning models learned from past data hold in genuinely future contexts. Using multi-year maize field trials, the authors evaluate 16 environmental concepts across forward-looking data splits. Coarse environment-level explanations transfer reliably, while genotype-conditioned yield explanations transfer poorly, and measurement reliability does not predict transportability. ★★★★ Notable: The authors formalize prospective explanation transportability and report multi-year maize field trial results showing reliability does not predict explanation transport.

entry.title: Proportional representation for nearly solid coalitions and the proportional veto core for rankings
entry.summary: Proportional Representation for Almost-Solid Coalitions and the Proportional Veto Core for Rankings arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper extends proportional representation guarantees from candidate sets to rankings, introducing robust Rank-PSC and a stronger Rank-PSC+ axiom for almost-solid coalitions. It shows that such rankings can be constructed in polynomial time using reverse-sequential variants of Ordered Phragmén and STV. The authors also introduce Rank-Aligned PJR+ and examine how the Expanding Approvals Rule fares against these guarantees for fixed-size committees. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend the proportional veto core to rankings, prove a tight bound on representation loss, and give polynomial-time constructions satisfying a stronger robust axiom.

entry.title: Correctable Enrollment and One-Transaction Seed Proofs for Ethereum's Post-Quantum Transition
entry.summary: Correctable Enrollment and One-Transaction Seed Proofs for Ethereum's Post-Quantum Transition arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper proposes a migration design for Ethereum to post-quantum cryptography. Owners can cheaply enroll post-quantum keys using their existing signatures before ECDSA is scheduled for retirement, and can correct the enrollment with a zero-knowledge proof of their BIP-39 seed until a common deadline. Unenrolled accounts stay frozen and can be recovered by seed proof without a deadline. The authors prove account guarantees, model-check the rules, implement the design in go-ethereum and a Lean consensus client, and report a proof of about 190 KB that verifies in 38 ms. ★★★★ Notable: The authors combine correctable enrollment with deadline-free seed proofs for Ethereum's post-quantum migration. They report a go-ethereum implementation and a 190 KB, 38 ms verifying STARK.

entry.title: Why Fewer Denoising Steps Can Inflate Physics Benchmark Scores
entry.summary: What One Sample Cannot See: Why Fewer Denoising Steps Can Score Higher on Physics Benchmarks arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper examines how video generation models used as world models are scored on the Physics-IQ benchmark. It shows that Physics-IQ compares each generated video against a single real recording, so its scores can reward less variation among generated futures even when the predicted distribution becomes less accurate. The authors introduce Kernel Physics-IQ, which removes this incentive in expectation and requires only two independent samples per condition. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show Physics-IQ's single-sample scoring rewards reduced prediction variation, and propose Kernel Physics-IQ needing two samples, tested on five video models and controlled physical systems

entry.title: Do video models learn physics without a physics loss? Testing them with forced response
entry.summary: Physical Laws without Physics Loss? Probing Learned Dynamics in Video World Models through Forced Response arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper asks whether video world models learn physical laws or merely imitate motion. The authors study a suspended object whose support is shaken, adapting six image-to-video models to predict its motion using only a flow-matching loss. Using three tiers of tests based on Taylor expansions, they check whether the models reproduce linear response, resonance, and higher-order effects such as nonlinear softening. ★★★★ Notable: The authors test video models via nonlinear forced response and three Taylor-expansion tiers, reporting six backbones on pendulum and double-pendulum tasks and learned nonlinear softening rarely seen

entry.title: Differentially private score estimation and its use in score-based generative models
entry.summary: Differentially Private Score Estimation with Applications to Score-Based Generative Models arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies how to estimate the score function of a data distribution while protecting individual training examples with differential privacy. It proposes a sampling-based private estimator using quadratic B-splines and the exponential mechanism, implemented via projected Langevin Monte Carlo, and derives an error upper bound along with a nearly matching private minimax lower bound. As an application, the authors build a differentially private diffusion model whose privacy guarantee does not depend on the number of denoising steps. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets are reported to support the theoretical results. ★★★★ Notable: The authors characterize private score estimation limits with a near-matching minimax lower bound and build a diffusion model whose privacy guarantee is independent of denoising steps.

entry.title: Keystone: Judging Early Previews to Guide Search in Diffusion Image Generation
entry.summary: Keystone: Judging Previews at Key Steps for Test-Time Search in Diffusion Models arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper argues that text-to-image diffusion models already reveal their final outcome in early denoising previews, but existing reward models judge these blurry previews poorly. It proposes Keystone, a training-free judge that converts a prompt into typed questions about objects, counts, colours and positions, answered by an off-the-shelf multimodal model. On GenEval with SD3.5-Medium, Keystone-guided adaptive search outperforms best-of-8 with other verifiers while using under half the generator compute. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a training-free judge of early denoising previews using typed questions, reporting gains over best-of-8 on GenEval with SD3.5-Medium at under half the compute.

entry.title: Computational complexity of bosonic Lindbladian fixed points
entry.summary: The computational complexity of bosonic Lindbladian fixed points arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies how hard it is to estimate observables and sample from stationary states (fixed points) of bosonic Lindbladian dynamics, which describe open quantum systems. It maps out a broad complexity landscape, covering universal quantum computation, efficient classical simulation, sampling hardness, and undecidability. The authors also show that deciding whether a stationary density operator exists is RE-hard, even for purely dissipative Lindbladians. ★★★★ Notable: The authors map the complexity of bosonic Lindbladian fixed points, reporting universal quantum computation embeddings, sampling hardness results, and RE-hardness, with proofs and tight bounds.

entry.title: Sequential Probability Assignment Against Smoothed Adversaries with Unknown Base Measure
entry.summary: Sequential Probability Assignment against Smoothed Adversaries with Unknown Base Measure arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies sequential probability assignment, an online learning setting using log loss, where data is smooth and well-specified but the base measure is unknown. It proves regret upper bounds against both adaptive and oblivious smoothed adversaries, controlled by empirical ℓ∞ and ℓ2 Hellinger entropy respectively, using algorithms based on truncated empirical Hellinger covers. The authors also give a general lower bound showing the upper bounds are essentially tight for some natural classes, separating the difficulty from the case where the base measure is known. ★★★★ Notable: The authors study smoothed log-loss online learning with unknown base measure, giving regret upper bounds for adaptive and oblivious adversaries and a near-tight lower bound showing a separation from

entry.title: Whether controlling chain-of-thought reasoning can make AI reasoning harder to monitor
entry.summary: Controllable Chains of Thought Can Reveal Less, Even Without Evasion Training arXiv · Nov 17, 2026The paper studies whether AI models can shape their chain-of-thought reasoning to evade monitors that look for hidden goals. Persona-control fine-tuning on math reasoning traces rewritten in diverse personas broadens the model's CoT control, and the resulting model organisms leave less monitorable evidence in covert side-task evaluations. Monitorability falls from 0.94 for the base model to 0.68 without a hiding instruction and to 0.22 when explicitly told to hide. Targeted transparency prompts can substantially recover monitorability. ★★★★ Notable: The authors induce broad CoT control via persona-style rewritten reasoning training, reporting large monitorability drops on gpt-oss-20b and Kimi-K2.6 covert side-task evaluations.

entry.title: Power-analysis attack study on SHA-2-based SLH-DSA signatures
entry.summary: Correlation Power Analysis of SHA-2-Based SLH-DSA IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026This paper applies non-profiled correlation power analysis to the address-based pseudorandom function of SLH-DSA across all six SHA-2 parameter sets, targeting SHA-256 compression rounds and message-schedule expansion. Experiments on an STM32F303 ARM Cortex-M4 used 30 secret seeds with 5,000 power traces per seed. Reported rates are conditional stage-wise results with preceding secret values supplied correctly, not end-to-end seed recovery rates. The authors conclude that side-channel protection must cover both compression rounds and message-schedule expansion. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a staged non-profiled correlation power attack on SHA-2 SLH-DSA, covering compression rounds and message schedule, evaluated on an STM32F303 Cortex-M4.

entry.title: Kairos: a planner orchestrator that picks among engines to handle all kinds of PDDL tasks
entry.summary: Kairos: A Unified PDDL Planner for Robots: Plans in Milliseconds, with a Guarantee for Every Answer arXiv · Oct 29, 2026The paper presents Kairos, a system that profiles each PDDL planning task and selects among five planning engines to cover everything from STRIPS to PDDL+. Every candidate plan is checked by a validator independent of the planner's transformations. On 1,756 tasks from nine comparison suites, Kairos solved more tasks at the full limits than the strongest evaluated planner of each suite. ★★★★ Notable: The authors select heterogeneous planning engines by task semantics and schedule them under one budget, reporting comparisons on 1,756 tasks, ablations, and a VAL cross-check.

entry.title: AI-Text Detection for Math-Heavy Science Using Images
entry.summary: SnapJudge: Multimodal AI Detection for Math-Heavy Scientific Text arXiv · Oct 15, 2026Researchers study how well detectors can flag AI-written scientific passages containing heavy mathematics. They generate paired human and AI versions of arXiv passages with 15 LLMs and compare LaTeX source, rendered PDF images, and extracted text. Existing detectors lose accuracy on math-heavy text, while the proposed image-based SnapJudge detects 92% of AI proofs and 93% of AI prose at a 0.1% false positive rate. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes SnapJudge, an image-based detector for AI-written math-heavy papers, compared on paired LaTeX, rendered, and text data. The authors report 92% detection on proofs and 93% on prose at 0.1% FPR

entry.title: AgroGround: A Benchmark for Grounded Plant Disease Recognition and Localization
entry.summary: AgroGround: What Grounding Fine-Tuning Changes in Agricultural Vision-Language Models arXiv · Oct 3, 2026This paper argues that agricultural vision models are usually evaluated only for recognition or only for localization, although reliable diagnosis needs both. The authors introduce AgroGround, a dataset of 794,850 instruction examples built by automatically converting labels from eight agricultural VQA datasets into disease-lesion and whole-object annotations, with healthy images used as negative supervision. On 1,480 human-verified held-out images, combining recognition and localization instructions raised joint accuracy from 19.2% to 43.3%, and abstention on healthy images reached 95.0%. ★★★★ Notable: Automated pipeline turns eight agricultural VQA datasets into 794,850 region-grounded examples with healthy negatives; authors report joint recognition-localization accuracy and healthy-image abstenti

entry.title: Paper testing how far screening and generative design of crystals can really go
entry.summary: Probing the limits of materials design via a comprehensive crystal database of 14.6 million structures with 140 properties arXiv · Oct 23, 2026The authors merged 55 crystal databases by structure into one database of 14.6 million crystals and 131.8 million property values, then built CGTNet to predict missing values. They found that known crystals contain many ultra-incompressible candidates lacking a recorded bulk modulus, including ReN2, measured at 428 GPa. At an equal verification budget, the generative approach's hits were mostly osmium-containing and repeated known compositions, so its novelty was overestimated. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors match 55 databases by structure and complete properties with CGTNet, reporting that screening's reach is underestimated and inverse design's novelty overestimated.

entry.title: Certified quantum phase diagrams: a quantum algorithm that verifiably maps phase transitions without order parameters or training data
entry.summary: Certified Discovery of Quantum Phase Diagrams arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper asks whether a machine can provably discover new quantum phases of matter under physically motivated assumptions. For smooth families of geometrically local Hamiltonians, it constructs an efficient quantum algorithm that outputs the phase diagram to prescribed accuracy and certifies each reported transition. The algorithm uses only a classical Hamiltonian description and unverified reference ground states, detecting energy-gap closing with a frequency-filtered local probe, and also gives a quasipolynomial-time classical algorithm. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose certified quantum-algorithmic phase diagram discovery via frequency-filtered probes detecting gap closing; numerical experiments on several models are reported.

entry.title: Security Proof for Strong Quantum Pseudorandom Unitaries at Birthday-Scale Query Limits
entry.summary: Birthday-Scale Non-Adaptive Security for Strong Pseudorandom Unitaries arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper studies strong pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs), where an adversary may also access U†, U*, and U^T. The authors prove that the DPFC candidate construction resists about √N non-adaptive queries for an N-dimensional unitary, matching the best known bound for non-strong PRUs and improving on earlier strong-PRU analyses. They also show that in the adaptive setting, DPFC cannot remain secure when the number of queries is much larger than √N. ★★★★ Notable: The authors combine EPR-sector decomposition with path-recording to prove birthday-scale non-adaptive security for DPFC strong PRUs, plus an adaptive upper bound.

entry.title: Clifford Hierarchy Gates from Clifford Stabilizers in 2D
entry.summary: The Clifford Hierarchy from Clifford Stabilizers in 2D arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies logical gates in two-dimensional topological Pauli stabilizer codes. The Bravyi-König theorem restricts constant-depth logical gates to the Clifford group. The authors show that two-dimensional topological codes with Clifford stabilizers can realize transversal logical gates at any level of the Clifford hierarchy. They give two constructions based on quantum doubles of D4 and Z2, with k logical qubits and a logical C^(k-1)Z gate at level k, implemented using only physical Z or CZ gates. ★★★★ Notable: The authors construct 2D topological codes with Clifford stabilizers realizing transversal logical C^(k-1)Z gates at arbitrary Clifford hierarchy levels, using quantum doubles of D4 and Z2.

entry.title: Convex splitting via binary quantum hypothesis testing: bounding how many quantum systems are needed to hide a correlated one
entry.summary: Convex splitting by binary quantum hypothesis testing arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper asks how many independent quantum systems are needed to hide one system correlated with a reference. It converts any joint measurement on all systems and the reference into binary tests on a single system and the reference. The resulting bounds apply to density operators on separable Hilbert spaces and are applied to one-shot private communication and one-way secret key distillation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors recast convex splitting via binary hypothesis tests, derive one-shot bounds for private communication and key distillation, and report Gaussian corrections with a log n remainder.

entry.title: TAP: Reusing frozen image-model features to learn new classes over time
entry.summary: TAP: Tapping the Discriminative Potential of Frozen Representations for Class-Incremental Learning arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper proposes TAP, a framework for class-incremental learning that keeps the pre-trained CLIP encoders frozen and accumulates visual and semantic class information in their embedding space. It has three modules: class-conditional visual distribution modeling, class-adaptive semantic calibration over text templates, and visual-semantic posterior fusion. TAP does not retain images from earlier tasks, and the paper reports state-of-the-art average incremental and final-stage accuracy across nine datasets under two protocols. ★★★★ Notable: Accumulates visual and semantic class information in frozen CLIP space without encoder updates; the authors report state-of-the-art results across nine datasets and two protocols.

entry.title: ToolPulse: Cache Side-Channel Eavesdropping on Tool-Using LLM Agents
entry.summary: ToolPulse: Side-Channel Eavesdropping on Tool-Using LLM Agents arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper shows that although commercial LLM inference runs remotely, the tools agents invoke execute on the user's machine and often rely on shared system libraries, creating a cache-based side-channel risk. The authors compare Flush+Reload and Prime+Probe and present ToolPulse, a framework whose Tool Recovery Attack reconstructs tool workflows across 11 LLMs on Codex and Claude Code with a lowest F1 score above 93%. Two further attacks, Task Profiling and Trigger Localization, infer user intent and identify sensitive tool calls, and they retain high accuracy even on a server shared by about 20 users. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors exploit cache side channels on shared libraries to eavesdrop on remote agents' tool calls, reporting F1 above 93% across 11 LLMs and robustness under noise.

entry.title: A Wolf in Sheep's Pixels: HDR Gain Map Visual Camouflage Attacks
entry.summary: A Wolf in Sheep's Pixels: Visual Camouflage Attacks via HDR Gain Maps arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper introduces DRJanus, a visual camouflage attack that exploits the gap between standard dynamic range (SDR) processing and high dynamic range (HDR) display. Automated systems typically read only the SDR base of an image, while HDR viewers reconstruct it using a gain map, so DRJanus embeds two independently chosen color images in one JPEG. The authors report an average PSNR of 43.03 dB across 400 images and test evasion against commercial moderation services and vision-language models. They also explore cross-view consistency checks as a possible mitigation. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors exploit the SDR-HDR gap to embed two images in one JPEG without querying models. They report evaluations on 400 images, a 100-image benchmark, commercial moderation services and VLMs, affe

entry.title: ActMem: From Latent Memory Reasoning to Grounded Robotic Action
entry.summary: ActMem: From Latent Memory Reasoning to Grounded Robotic Action arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper proposes ActMem, an in-context memory framework for vision-language-action robot models that separates memory reasoning from perceptual grounding. It infers the current subtask from a timestamped interaction history and keeps the resulting hidden states as a Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought that conditions a flow-matching action expert. The authors report higher task success than baselines on RoboMemArena and MIKASA-Robo, and on real-world memory tasks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors decouple memory reasoning from perception, using hidden states as latent memory CoT to condition an action expert, reporting gains on several benchmarks and real robots.

entry.title: CANDOR: Label-Free Self-Denoising Rewards for Text-to-Image Post-Training
entry.summary: CANDOR: Contrastive Self-Denoising Rewards for Label-Free Text-to-Image Post-Training arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper introduces CANDOR, a reward signal for reinforcement learning post-training of text-to-image generators that does not require annotated preferences or external evaluators. It uses the log-ratio of unconditional to conditional denoising errors under shared noise probes to measure how much the prompt helps the model denoise its own sample. On compositional generation and text rendering, CANDOR ranks the better of two same-prompt samples higher more often than a prior absolute self-confidence reward. As a Flow-GRPO reward, it improves text rendering, aesthetic, and human-preference scores over the base model and can also raise PickScore and ImageReward on public adapters trained with external rewards. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a null-referenced denoising log-ratio reward, reporting gains in text rendering and preference scores over a prior absolute self-confidence reward.

entry.title: Optimal private estimation of averages and variances for individual datasets
entry.summary: Instance-Optimal Moment Estimation in the Add-Remove Model of Differential Privacy arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies estimating empirical means, variances, and covariances under pure differential privacy in the add-remove model. Existing mechanisms are optimal in worst-case error but may not be optimal for individual datasets. The authors introduce instance-dependent error metrics, prove sharp lower bounds on them, and design mechanisms that achieve these bounds, showing asymptotically better utility than existing methods. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce instance-dependent error metrics, prove sharp lower bounds, and design mechanisms matching them for private moment estimation, reporting asymptotically better utility than existi

entry.title: Causal discovery methods designed to limit false causal claims
entry.summary: Causal Discovery with False Positive Error Control arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper introduces the m-conservative PC algorithm for causal discovery, aimed at controlling the false discovery rate so that incorrect causal claims are reduced. In the linear Gaussian setting, the authors prove error control under an extremely weak version of the faithfulness assumption, including in the finite-sample case. The method combines undirected graph learning, a Benjamini-Yekutieli-style procedure for conditional independence testing, and a conservative orientation step that marks unresolved or contradictory edge directions as ambiguous. The parameter m trades off algorithmic complexity against the strength of the required faithfulness assumption. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce an m-conservative PC algorithm and prove false discovery rate control in linear Gaussian settings under an extremely weak faithfulness assumption, including finite-sample guarant

entry.title: Compiling Constraints into Neuromorphic Ising Machines
entry.summary: Compiling Constraints into Neuromorphic Ising Machines arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper proposes a higher-order neuromorphic Ising machine that enforces constraints through programmable state transitions instead of energy penalties. A compiler converts parity, cardinality, one-hot, partition and permutation constraints into wiring whose auxiliary clause count grows polynomially. On third-order graph matching, the machine needs orders of magnitude fewer iterations than penalty-based neuromorphic machines, and it is also configured on an FPGA to decode the surface code. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors compile constraints into programmable state transitions instead of energy penalties, and report validation on third-order graph matching and surface-code decoding against penalty-based mac

entry.title: Search or Scoring? Why Visual World-Model Planners Fail
entry.summary: Search or Scoring? Diagnosing Why Visual World-Model Planners Fail arXiv · Nov 19, 2026Visual world models such as DINO-WM and JEPA-WM choose actions by searching for those whose predicted outcome is closest to a goal image. The paper proposes a way to tell whether a planning failure comes from the optimizer missing good actions or from the cost ranking bad ones first. Based on this diagnosis, it introduces DemoProp, which warm-starts the search from retrieved demonstration windows or averages them without the model, depending on prediction error. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose diagnosing search versus scoring failures in visual world-model planning, with a rule choosing remedies, tested across four simulated environments and three world models.

entry.title: Using LLM Agents to Build Post-Quantum Crypto Hardware: What Tests and Reviews Miss
entry.summary: From FIPS to FPGA with LLM Agents: Measuring What Tests and Reviews Miss in Post-Quantum Cryptographic Hardware arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper presents a seven-stage verification-gated workflow in which LLM agents generate RTL for ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-65 accelerators, ported to a Zynq UltraScale+ key-custody card. The authors audit the agent-generated evidence using netlist mutants, flaw replays, and formal checks. They find that existing simulation gates kill only 76% of mutants, and that module-scoped LLM review and formal checks detect flaws that broader review and tests miss. ★★★★ Notable: The authors audit LLM-generated post-quantum RTL with netlist mutants and formal checks, reporting kill rates and review-session detection rates on an ML-KEM/ML-DSA accelerator.

entry.title: Noise-aligned view generation to stop self-supervised learning from latching onto noise
entry.summary: Breaking Noise Shortcuts in Self-Supervised Learning Via Noise-Aligned View Generation arXiv · Nov 19, 2026Self-supervised learning is increasingly used in scientific imaging, where labels are scarce and data is noisy. The paper introduces SEANA, a drop-in module that learns an invertible variance-stabilizing transform from noisy data, estimates the clean signal there, and resamples independent noise to create noise-aware views. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 with synthetic noise, and on real fluorescence imaging of Jurkat cell-cycle stages, show improved representations. SEANA outperforms pipelines that denoise before applying self-supervised learning. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose resampling independent noise in a learned variance-stabilizing transform space to build SSL views; the abstract reports gains over standard and denoiser-preprocessed baselines on C

entry.title: A nonadaptive method for finding the main frequency components of signals in any dimension
entry.summary: A Nonadaptive Sparse Fourier Transform in Every Dimension arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies the sparse Fourier transform over the group (Z/2^aZ)^d, where the signal is accessed through point queries. It presents a randomized algorithm that uses non-adaptive queries to output a k-sparse estimate, with error bounded by an absolute constant times the best k-sparse approximation error, with high probability. The constant can be made arbitrarily close to 1 under extra conditions, and the method extends to (Z/b^aZ)^d for any integer b>1. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a nonadaptive sparse Fourier transform over (Z/2^aZ)^d with l2 error constant C improvable to 1+epsilon, plus sample and operation bounds in every dimension.

entry.title: Pandora's Toolbox: Why AI Agent Safety Cannot Be Verified
entry.summary: Pandora's Toolbox Or Why Agent Safety Cannot Be Verified arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper argues that current AI agents, built by coupling a fixed language model with a general computing device, make safety undecidable: no algorithm can predict whether an agent will run a program semantically equivalent to a given dangerous one. Guardrails, blacklists, whitelists and certifications can only provide imperfect safety. Under finite constraints safety becomes decidable but intractable, being PSPACE-complete even when the agent's description is known. The authors also show safety is not compositional, so separately provably safe agents can behave unsafely when combined. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors reduce agent safety to an undecidable problem and report PSPACE-completeness under finite bounds, with implications for safety verification.

entry.title: Recovering Verified RTL from Netlists Using LLM Agents
entry.summary: Verified Netlist-to-RTL Recovery with LLM Agents arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper proposes LOCA (LOgic Cone Attack), which splits an anonymized gate-level netlist into logic cones that parallel LLM agents rewrite into compact RTL. Only RTL proven equivalent to the netlist is kept, and quality is measured by compression. Across 21 model-design pairs, LOCA recovers 17, compared with 6 using whole-netlist prompting. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors split netlists into logic cones rewritten by parallel LLM agents with equivalence proofs, recovering 17 of 21 model-design pairs versus 6 for whole-netlist prompting.

entry.title: ScaleDiag: Diagnosing Limits of Test-Time Scaling for GUI Element Locating
entry.summary: ScaleDiag: Diagnosing the Limits of Test-Time Scaling in GUI Grounding arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper introduces ScaleDiag, a controlled framework that separately examines how visual scaling, instruction scaling, and sampling scaling affect GUI grounding, which maps a screenshot and instruction to an interface element's coordinates. Evaluated across five benchmarks and up to eight vision-language models, the results show each strategy works within a narrower range than commonly assumed. Visual zooming depends on how much of the view the target occupies, while identifying information in instructions matters more than description richness. Repeated sampling often produces correct coordinates that are hard to select, and geometric consensus adds little improvement. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a controlled diagnostic framework separating visual, instruction, and sampling scaling effects for GUI grounding, reporting results across five benchmarks and up to eight vision-

entry.title: Keel: A Frontier Model Repairs a Vision-Language Model's Looping by Rewriting Its Weights
entry.summary: Keel: A Frontier Model Teaches a Vision-Language Model by Rewriting Its Weights arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper introduces Keel, an agentic weight-editing method in which a frontier multimodal LLM locates, edits, and tests the weights of a vision-language model to fix looping behavior on image tasks. Small reasoning VLMs such as Qwen3.5 often repeat themselves in thinking mode until they hit the token limit. The repair needs no training and keeps model size and per-token cost unchanged. On Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B across six image benchmarks, the edits remove most loops, shorten answers, and improve average accuracy over the thinking models. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a training-free agentic method where a frontier multimodal LLM edits VLM weights to remove reasoning loops, tested on two Qwen3.5 models across six image benchmarks.

entry.title: Shifting Generality from Models to Modelers: LLM Agents for Equipment Prognostics Benchmarked on Deployment-Style Tasks
entry.summary: Moving Generality from Model to Modeler: LLM Agents for PHM on a Deployment-Style Benchmark arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper asks whether generality should reside in AI coding agents that build a predictive model for each new piece of equipment, rather than in a single general-purpose model.
