The authors introduce NextUnit-Bench, a deployment-style benchmark for prognostics and health management with 24 public datasets split into 58 folds of held-out units or operating conditions. They find that frontier agents outperform AutoML and reproduced published methods, that their advantage comes from data-driven design, and that a short plain-text plan can transfer much of that advantage to weaker implementers who must still execute it.| ★★★★ Notable: The authors shift generality from models to modeling agents, reporting on a 24-dataset, 58-fold deployment benchmark comparing agents, AutoML, and published methods, plus plan-transfer and open-weight

entry.title: Recurrent vision-language models for tracking hidden objects in video
entry.summary: Recurrent Vision Language Models Solve the Shell Game arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies how vision language models struggle to track a hidden object through video, using the shell game as the test task. The authors propose RecurrentVLM, which makes each attention layer of a pretrained model recur over time by computing keys and values from the outputs of finished frame groups. The reported results show near-perfect accuracy on two benchmarks and on 50-swap games after training on at most 30 swaps. ★★★★ Notable: The authors make each attention layer of a pretrained VLM recur over time to track hidden objects in the shell game. They report high accuracy on VET-Bench, MET-Bench, and 50-swap games, suggesting re

entry.title: Identity World Model: Recognizing People by Imagining Their Features Under Changed Conditions
entry.summary: Identity World Model: Recognizing People in an Imagined Latent World arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper proposes IDWorld, an identity world model for whole-body human recognition that predicts how a person would be represented under changed conditions, rather than relying on cues like clothing or pose. It imagines features under shared canonical conditions in a single forward pass without rendering pixels, and adaptively fuses these imagined conditions for each probe-gallery pair. The authors report state-of-the-art or strong results on several benchmarks, including CCPG, CCGR-MINI, MEVID, CASIA-B*, SUSTech1K, and CCVID. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply latent world modeling to person recognition, imagining canonical-condition features and adaptively fusing them; the paper reports state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks.

entry.title: When AI Analysts Disagree: Robustness Checks of Research Findings Using AI Agents
entry.summary: When AI Analysts Disagree: Agentic Multiverse Analysis and the Robustness of Empirical Research arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper proposes an agentic multiverse analysis framework in which AI agents list the defensible analytical choices in a study, score them for validity, and run the resulting specifications. A pilot with 150 autonomous coding agents on one dataset found they disagreed through methodological choices similar to those of human analysts. Applied to ten empirical studies from a leading management journal's replication packages, comprising 1,755 specification estimates, the framework reproduced the original estimates and showed that some conclusions hold across all validated specifications while others depend on individual analytical choices the papers do not discuss. ★★★★ Notable: The authors combine multiverse analysis with autonomous AI agents to enumerate analytical forks, reproducing original estimates across ten management studies and revealing sensitivities the texts omit

entry.title: Blind spots transfer, knowledge does not: what RL inherits from an LLM judge
entry.summary: Blind Spots Travel, Knowledge Stays Home: What RL Inherits from an LLM Judge arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper examines, across 814 reinforcement learning runs training 7-8B models to answer closed-book questions or abstain, what knowledge an LLM judge passes to the trained model. The judge's knowledge about individual answers does not transfer, but its beliefs about a category of questions do. For example, a judge rejecting eleven of twelve correct answers about capitals of former states led the model to refuse 98% of such capitals on new questions. Rewarding the answer that most untrained samples agree on, with no labels and no judge, earned the same reward as the answer key and kept the category intact. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors separate single-answer knowledge from category beliefs, reporting 814 RL runs where category-level beliefs transfer and cause refusals across a whole question type.

entry.title: AI-driven multiverse analysis tests how robust finance papers reusing natural experiments are
entry.summary: An AI-Powered Multiverse Analysis of Empirical Finance Research: Evidence from Reused Natural Experiments arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper uses AI agents to reanalyze 324 finance papers that reuse 13 natural experiments, rebuilding their data and reproducing each main estimate. The agents re-estimate the effects across 62,409 defensible specifications to build measures of empirical robustness. The authors reproduce 42% of signed main estimates under the papers' own specifications, and on average about 25% of all defensible specifications keep the published sign with p < 0.10. ★★★★ Notable: The authors run an AI-agent multiverse analysis of 324 papers across 62,409 specifications, reporting 42% main-estimate reproduction and systematic robustness measures.

entry.title: CoMPASS: A Benchmark Testing Whether AI Chatbots Encourage Users' Emotional Attachment
entry.summary: CoMPASS: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Measuring LLM Reinforcement of Parasocial Behavior arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper introduces CoMPASS, a multi-turn benchmark that measures whether conversational LLMs reinforce or resist users' gradually escalating parasocial attachment. It is grounded in attachment theory and uses four user personas, three escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency), and a seven-signal scoring rubric. The authors tested eight frontier models from four providers and found that multi-turn escalation raised parasocial behavior scores across all models. Differences between providers were larger than differences within the same provider, suggesting provider-level choices such as post-training matter more than model scale. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a multi-turn benchmark grounded in attachment theory, reporting results across eight frontier models that suggest provider-level post-training shapes parasocial reinforcement.

entry.title: MAWAM: A multi-agent model that predicts robot team actions and their future views together for coordinated manipulation.
entry.summary: MAWAM: A Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Coordinated Manipulation arXiv · Nov 19, 2026MAWAM is a multi-agent world-action model for coordinated robot manipulation. It jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample, built from a pretrained single-robot backbone and using cross-agent attention. It reports 67.8% mean success on three real-robot tasks, 18.9 points above MA-VLA, and 90.3% mean success on eight simulated tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations indicate that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control. ★★★★ Notable: The authors jointly denoise multiple robots' actions and future views via cross-agent attention, reporting real-robot and simulation success rates with ablations.

entry.title: Abusing browser-embedded local language models for post-exploitation attacks
entry.summary: Living off the Local Model: Abusing Browser-Embedded Language Models for Post-Exploitation arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper examines whether language models built into browsers, such as Gemini Nano in Chrome, could be used by attackers after they gain access to a host. The authors report that the model can be driven using only interpreters that ship with the operating system, and that the user-activation check before download can be satisfied with a simulated click or bypassed. They also measure the model's ability to find credentials, detect PII in email, classify images, and call custom tools. Combining these abilities, they carry out a simulated operation with no user interaction. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show browser-embedded local models can serve as post-exploitation engines, bypassing the activation check, and report capability tests plus an end-to-end simulated operation.

entry.title: Near-quadratic sample compression for all VC classes
entry.summary: Near-Quadratic Sample Compression for All VC Classes arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper addresses a long-open problem in learning theory: whether every binary concept class with VC dimension d admits a sample compression scheme whose size depends only on d. The best previous bound, by Moran and Yehudayoff, was exponential in d. The authors construct a compression scheme of size O(d² log² d), proving the weaker polynomial-size version of the conjecture. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors improve the exponential compression bound to near-quadratic O(d^2 log^2 d), proving the weaker sample compression conjecture for all VC classes.

entry.title: Signed, Valid, and Unauthorized: Wallet-Side Checks for Agent Stablecoin Payments
entry.summary: Signed, Valid, and Unauthorized: Authority Closure at the Trust Boundary Between Agent Commerce Protocols and Crypto Wallets arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper examines how wallets signing objects for agent commerce payments in stablecoins can grant transfer permissions beyond what the buyer approved. The authors define authority closure as all transfer sequences a signed object can enable and build Closure, a wallet-side checker covering 13 families of signed objects. In an evaluation of 2,130 generated objects, Closure rejected all objects with an observed violation and accepted the rest. The median decision time was at most 12 microseconds per family. ★★★★ Notable: The authors define authority closure for signed wallet objects, characterize when they respect the mandate, and report a 13-family checker evaluated on generated objects and x402 clients.

entry.title: Trace2ST: Using LLMs to Rebuild PLC Structured Text Programs from I/O Logs and Verify Them
entry.summary: Trace2ST: Recovering PLC Structured Text from I/O Traces with LLM Generation and Verification arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper examines whether a large language model can recover an executable Structured Text program for PLCs using only logged input and output traces, and how to verify the result. The authors propose a generate-replay-feedback pipeline and evaluate it on 47 third-party programs from two public benchmarks. In 43 cases the recovered program exactly reproduces the recorded trace, and it agrees with the original on 94% of scans for unseen inputs. On real data from a public water-treatment testbed, the recovered control laws closely match unseen measurements (R² > 0.99). ★★★★ Notable: The authors recover Structured Text PLC programs from I/O traces using an LLM with replay-feedback verification, reporting high agreement on 47 programs and a water-treatment testbed.

entry.title: When Program Structure Is Required: Certificate-Grounded Calibration of Program-Induction Difficulty
entry.summary: When Is Program Structure Required? Certificate-Grounded Calibration of Program-Induction Difficulty arXiv · Nov 17, 2026The paper introduces certificate-grounded calibration, which builds matched tasks in a bounded string-replacement language whose minimum solutions use one rule or two rules. Exhaustive one-rule enumeration and an executable two-rule witness verify the difference before any model inference. The authors evaluate 120 reference families using 1,440 new and 480 saved model trajectories. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce certificate-grounded calibration separating one- and two-rule program-induction tasks, reporting experiments across 120 families and two models.

entry.title: HireWatch: Testing whether LLMs follow U.S. hiring law under pressure
entry.summary: HireWatch: Evaluating LLM Compliance with U.S. Employment Law Under Contextual Pressure arXiv · Nov 16, 2026This paper introduces HireWatch, a benchmark that tests whether large language models follow U.S. laws limiting what questions employers may ask job candidates. The authors built a 200-question bank of lawful and unlawful interview questions, classified using U.S. federal statutes, regulations, and agency guidance. Across 18 closed and open-weight models and about 100,000 trials, models mostly avoided unlawful questions in low-pressure settings, but violations rose sharply under higher pressure. Explicit instructions to comply with the law improved compliance but did not fully eliminate violations. ★★★★ Notable: The authors evaluate 18 LLMs over about 100,000 trials, reporting that unlawful interview question selection rises under higher contextual pressure.

entry.title: A quantum master equation that keeps detailed balance and has second-order error bounds
entry.summary: A Nonsecular Quantum Master Equation with Detailed Balance and Second-order Error Bound arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper constructs a nonsecular quantum master equation for open quantum systems that satisfies time-reversal Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (TR-KMS) detailed balance, inherited from microscopic reversibility. Under suitable conditions, the authors prove that the difference between predicted and exact reduced density matrices is bounded by O(λ²) uniformly in time, where λ is the system-bath coupling strength. In a benchmark with two coupled oscillators, the equation keeps O(λ²) accuracy in both secular and nonsecular regimes and outperforms the other detailed-balance equations tested. ★★★★ Notable: The authors construct a nonsecular master equation with TR-KMS detailed balance, report a time-uniform O(λ²) error bound, and validate it on a two-oscillator benchmark.

entry.title: Limits of magic-state cultivation: which faults harm non-Clifford state preparation
entry.summary: The limits of magic-state cultivation arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper develops an exact theory of which faults are harmful in circuits that prepare magic states with non-Clifford gates and postselection, such as magic-state cultivation. It shows that a single stabilizer code on the non-Clifford gates determines harmful faults, linking cultivation to distillation and bounding the T-count from below. The authors also show that using S gates as a proxy for T gates can only overstate the fault distance of such checks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors develop an exact theory identifying harmful faults via one stabilizer code, giving a T-count lower bound and analyzing magic-state cultivation checks.

entry.title: On reaction depth and fast fault-tolerant Boolean logic (paper on classical-coprocessor consultations in quantum programs)
entry.summary: On Reaction Depth and Fast Fault-Tolerant Boolean Logic arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper formalizes “reaction depth,” the number of times a classical coprocessor must be consulted while running a quantum program, and examines subtleties in this theory. It focuses on coherent Boolean logic and uses a gateset of homogeneous Z- and X-type Pauli product measurements plus Toffoli states. The authors prove that any Boolean arithmetic circuit can be implemented with constant quantum depth and constant reaction depth, at the cost of exponential space. They also present efficient AutoAND, ripple-carry adder, and schoolbook multiplier implementations. ★★★★ Notable: The authors formalize reaction depth, prove any Boolean arithmetic circuit has constant quantum and reaction depth, and give efficient adder and multiplier constructions.

entry.title: A provably efficient classical method for simulating first-order OTOCs in 1D
entry.summary: A provably efficient classical algorithm for simulating OTOC⁽¹⁾ in 1D arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper introduces "window propagation," a classical algorithm for approximating first-order out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) in 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits. The authors prove it runs in polynomial time at arbitrary depths, with inverse-polynomial mean-squared error. Numerical experiments compare its results with exact computation on Clifford circuits with up to 512 qubits and 768 T-gates, and on Haar-random circuits with up to 22 qubits. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce window propagation, claiming the first provably polynomial-time classical approximation of first-order OTOCs in 1D Haar brickwork circuits, with numerical comparisons up to 512 q

entry.title: Measurement-order dependence and limits on quantum uncertainty, contextuality, steering and Bell violations
entry.summary: Measurement-order dependence bounds uncertainty, contextuality, steering, and Bell nonlocality arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper measures how much the outcome statistics change when two quantum measurements are performed in opposite orders, using total-variation, Jensen-Shannon and Hellinger distances. These order scores vanish when the measurements commute. The authors use them to bound violations of noncontextuality, steering and Bell inequalities. ★★★★ Notable: The authors bound Bell violations bilinearly by order-record distances, prove the bound for one party with up to three settings, and conjecture it in general.

entry.title: Impossibility theorems for ordered universal entanglement purification
entry.summary: No-Go Theorems for Ordered Universal Entanglement Purification arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies whether nontrivial universal entanglement purification is possible for a finite set of pairs with ordered fidelities, using separable operations. For each fixed number of inputs, it shows that when independently prepared two-qubit pairs range over all states above a fixed fidelity threshold, any successful map that never lowers the highest input fidelity must preserve that fidelity exactly. This rules out nontrivial universal LOCC purification even at arbitrarily high input fidelities. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove a no-go theorem for ordered universal purification under separable operations, for every finite n and arbitrarily high input fidelity.

entry.title: Long-distance continuous-variable entanglement distribution over deployed fibre
entry.summary: Long-distance continuous variable entanglement distribution over deployed fibre arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper demonstrates distributing continuous-variable entanglement over deployed metropolitan optical fibre. The two modes of a two-mode squeezed vacuum state are sent to remote nodes through 23 km (about 7 dB loss) and 450 m (about 1 dB loss) fibre links, each using an independent free-running laser and a polarisation-diverse coherent receiver. Digital recovery of timing, phase and polarisation uses co-propagating pilot tones, and inter-mode correlations align the quadratures. The entanglement is certified by a Simon-Duan value of 1.915 ± 0.013, below the separability bound of 2, and a logarithmic negativity of 0.067 ± 0.011. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report distributing CV entanglement over deployed metro fibre using digital recovery of phase, polarisation and timing, verified via Simon-Duan and log negativity.

entry.title: Topological origin of directional amplification in higher-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices
entry.summary: Topological Origin of Directional Amplification in Arbitrary-Dimensional Non-Hermitian Lattices arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies directional amplification in non-Hermitian lattices, where gain, loss and nonreciprocal couplings can produce exponentially growing responses. Using the concept of the amoeba, the logarithmic image of the singularities of the response generating function, the authors build a framework valid in any dimension. They show that the asymptotic response is determined by the component of the amoeba's complement extending toward negative infinity, giving a general topological criterion for whether directional amplification occurs. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use amoeba connected components to give a dimension-independent topological criterion for directional amplification in non-Hermitian lattices.

entry.title: Fast exact noisy quantum circuit sampling with mid-circuit measurements and general noise channels
entry.summary: General Noise Channels and Mid-Circuit Measurements for Pre-Trajectory Sampling with Batched Execution arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper generalizes pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution (PTSBE) to noisy quantum circuits with mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels, without approximation. Implemented on GPUs as a CUDA-Q extension, it reports speedups of up to 24x over conventional CUDA-Q trajectory sampling on distance-3 topological code memories and up to 83x over the Clifft simulator on 30-qubit random circuits. The authors also find that Pauli twirling of amplitude damping overestimates the detection rate by 21% and raises a lookup decoder's logical error rate by 8% on a surface-code memory. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend pre-trajectory sampling to mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels, reporting speedups over CUDA-Q and Clifft on GPUs.

entry.title: A fault-tolerant quantum chip needing few external control wires
entry.summary: Fault-tolerant quantum processor with minimal external control arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper proposes a fault-tolerant architecture for universal quantum computation, inspired by classical processors, where quantum information flows through a fixed, clocked planar array of local gates. The chip receives classical instructions through a small, constant number of external wires, while other qubits evolve under a fixed, periodically applied depth-3 local circuit. Assuming a noiseless global clock, the authors establish an accuracy threshold theorem. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a fault-tolerant quantum processor with few external wires and a fixed depth-3 local circuit, and report an accuracy threshold theorem.

entry.title: Sharp Complexity Thresholds for Network Cournot Competition (how hard it is to compute equilibria in networked firm markets)
entry.summary: Sharp Complexity Thresholds for Network Cournot Competition arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper determines how hard it is to approximate network Cournot equilibria, depending on demand polynomial degree and the number of firms per market. Cubic demands are polynomial-time solvable at high precision for any market size, while quartic and quintic demands remain tractable with at most three and two firms per market. Beyond these thresholds, approximation is shown to be PPAD-hard. The paper also gives a polynomial-time algorithm for arbitrary-degree nonincreasing concave polynomial demands when each firm's cost depends only on its total production. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report exact complexity thresholds for network Cournot equilibrium approximation, tied to demand degree and firms per market, with PPAD-hardness and a polynomial-time algorithm.

entry.title: Optimal online auction competitive ratio for subadditive valuations is below 1/2
entry.summary: The Optimal Competitive Ratio for Subadditive Online Combinatorial Auctions is Less Than 1/2 arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper builds a four-buyer online combinatorial auction with independent subadditive valuations and a fixed, known arrival order. In this instance, every online rule earns strictly less than half the expected offline optimum. The paper computes the optimal online and offline welfare exactly and shows that a 1/2 guarantee always holds with at most three buyers. ★★★★ Notable: The authors construct a four-buyer subadditive online combinatorial auction counterexample showing the optimal competitive ratio is below 1/2, contrasting with a 1/2 guarantee for three buyers.

entry.title: General progress can stand in for withheld training data in language models
entry.summary: General progress substitutes for specific training data in language models arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper examines what happens when a language model's training omits data for a specific skill. Experiments on chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages and web text show that a model's general progress on other training data can substitute for the withheld data. When retrained on the withheld data later, models acquire the skill using a small fraction of the data needed initially, and that fraction shrinks as models improve. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors show general progress substitutes for withheld training data, testing chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages, web text, and a 7B model's programming language.

entry.title: Does the Action Matter? Testing If Driving World Models Use Their Actions
entry.summary: Does the Action Matter? Probing Action-Conditioned Semantic Forecasting as a World Model for Autonomous Driving arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper examines whether action-conditioned semantic forecasting models for autonomous driving actually depend on the ego vehicle's action when predicting future scenes. The authors compare forecasters with action conditioning against identical models without action input, using test-time action interventions scored by segmentation metrics. Experiments in a synthetic environment and on Cityscapes and BDD100K show that wrong actions substantially degrade predictions while correct actions yield only modest gains. ★★★★ Notable: The authors test action dependence in driving world models via test-time action interventions, validated on Cityscapes, BDD100K, and a synthetic environment.

entry.title: What Survival Benchmarks Miss: How Model Selection and Dataset Conditions Shape Results
entry.summary: What Survival Benchmarks Don't Tell You: Impact of Model Selection and Dataset Regimes arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper compares 10 classical, tree-based, and deep learning survival analysis methods across 49 datasets, treating the model selection criterion as a separate experimental variable. It finds that tuning hyperparameters for the Integrated Brier Score instead of the C-index improves probabilistic accuracy and calibration for complex models with little loss in ranking ability. The authors argue that evaluation design and dataset characteristics strongly affect conclusions, so results should transparently report the evaluation setup. ★★★★ Notable: The authors treat the model selection criterion as an independent variable, benchmarking 10 methods on 49 datasets with Bayesian mixed-effects modeling and showing evaluation design shapes conclusions

entry.title: The Elephant in the Question: How Unified Models Visualize Concepts Behind Answers
entry.summary: The Elephant in the Question: Unified Models Picture the Concepts Behind Their Answers arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper introduces V-lens, a method that uses the image generator of unified multimodal models to visualize a chosen token's hidden state without training a separate decoder. Tests across four diffusion-based and two autoregressive models show the images reveal intermediate concepts linking a question to its answer, even when those concepts are never named. The authors also propose lens tuning, which supervises selected hidden states with pictures, raising correct visualization of pronoun referents from 2-11% to 86-94% on three models. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose V-lens, visualizing hidden states via unified models' image generators without training a decoder, plus lens tuning with picture supervision; reported pronoun-referent accuracy ris

entry.title: Counterfactual World Models: JEPAs for "What If" Reasoning
entry.summary: Counterfactual World Models: JEPAs That Reason About "What If" arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper asks whether world models can answer counterfactual questions, such as what would have happened under a different action with the same hidden disturbance. The authors prove that models trained only on factual transitions cannot answer this alone. For many physical systems, they propose a first-order method that adds the difference between predictions under alternative and factual actions to the observed outcome, requiring no counterfactual data or retraining. Tested on pixel-based simulators with JEPA models, the approach substantially raises counterfactual R² and outperforms an oracle planner in hindsight planning. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a JEPA-based counterfactual world model using only factual data, with an O(h²) error bound and matching minimax lower bound, tested on five simulators.

entry.title: 4D-TEMPO: a differentiable method that fits atoms directly to electron-microscope data, with per-atom error bars
entry.summary: 4D-TEMPO: Differentiable 4D-STEM ptychography via fast Physics Optimizers arXiv · Nov 19, 2026The paper presents 4D-TEMPO, a differentiable physical renderer that fits atom positions, microscope and detector parameters directly to recorded electron counts under a Poisson likelihood. Its output lists each atom with a 3D position, thermal width, and a model-conditional error bar derived from the Fisher information. On a simulated WSe₂ bilayer it reduced in-plane error by about one third and depth error by 40-61% relative to the published reconstruction, and on experimental WSe₂ it predicted held-out patterns better than three published codes. ★★★★ Notable: The authors fit atoms, microscope and detector directly under a Poisson likelihood with a differentiable renderer and report per-atom Fisher error bars, validated on simulated and experimental WSe2 ag

entry.title: Elysium: Simulation-Free Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridges for Cell Dynamics
entry.summary: Elysium: Simulation-Free Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridges arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper introduces Elysium, a method for reconstructing cellular dynamics from snapshot data, jointly learning state transitions and changes in population size from proliferation and apoptosis. It uses a killed Brownian reference process and its time reversal to build direct regression objectives without simulating trajectories during training. On simulated benchmarks and single-cell time courses, Elysium outperforms existing deterministic and bridge-based solvers. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a simulation-free unbalanced Schrödinger bridge solver jointly learning state transitions and mass change, validated on simulated benchmarks and single-cell time courses for cellul

entry.title: Learning the Anyon Atlas: Searching for Modular Data of 2+1D Topological Quantum Field Theories
entry.summary: Learning the Anyon Atlas arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper extends the search for modular data of 2+1 dimensional topological quantum field theories from 22 to 42 anyons, identifying 150,679 new modular data sets. The authors add three rejection gates to their algorithm, two based on logistic regression, to discard unlikely representations. Using this data, they find counterexamples to a Geiko-Moore conjecture on time-reversal symmetry in Chern-Simons theories and propose a refined criterion. ★★★★ Notable: The authors add logistic-regression gates to extend the search to rank 42, report 150,679 new modular data, counterexamples to the Geiko-Moore conjecture, and rank-100 prime data.

entry.title: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Test Environments for Scientific Discovery AI Agents
entry.summary: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper introduces Openhagen Worlds, a suite of 27 procedurally generated environments, ranging from classic experimental reasoning puzzles to simulator-based physics and chemistry. Agents run experiments under a budget and commit an answer, which a deterministic verifier checks against a hidden truth. Each difficulty level is calibrated, with core and frontier tiers. On frontier instances, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash shows substantial remaining headroom, especially in eight-stage campaigns, and expert iteration gives a 9B model modest gains. ★★★★ Notable: The authors build 27 calibrated environments for scientific discovery agents, gating levels with oracle and shortcut policies. They report frontier model evaluations on 84 withheld instances and exper

entry.title: Capacity of a random-bag communication channel with and without feedback
entry.summary: The Asymptotic Capacity of the Grabbag Channel With and Without Feedback arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies communication through a randomly mixed store called the Grabbag channel. Each use inserts a ball of one of K colors into a bag of M balls, then one of the resulting M+1 balls is chosen uniformly, observed, and removed. The authors show that for 2 ≤ K ≤ M+1, both the no-feedback capacity and the capacity with noiseless strictly causal output feedback are at most 9.77(K/(M+1))^{2/3}. For M+1 ≥ 2^22 both are at least an absolute constant times (K/(M+1))^{2/3}, so both are of order (K/M)^{2/3}. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give matching-order bounds of (K/(M+1))^{2/3} on the capacity with and without feedback, with proofs for both directions.

entry.title: Stealing exact private training data from other clients in federated learning
entry.summary: Stealing Exact Training Data from Other Clients during Federated Learning arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper presents an attack pipeline in which a malicious client uses model updates from federated learning to reconstruct other clients' private text. The method iteratively subtracts the gradient contributions of sentences already recovered exactly, exposing the remaining sentences for recovery in later rounds. The authors report the first exact sentence recovery with 100% precision, recovering up to 80.2% of client sentences exactly on aggregates with up to 4 times more tokens than the model's hidden dimension. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a new iterative attack unwinding FedAvg gradient entanglement, recovering up to 80.2% of client sentences exactly.

entry.title: Proof that diffusion models are efficient priors for recovering sparse signals
entry.summary: Diffusion Models are Provably Efficient Priors for Sparse Recovery arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies recovering a sparse signal from a few linear measurements, a classic compressed sensing problem, using a pretrained diffusion model as a prior. It shows that if the diffusion model accurately captures a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli-Gaussian prior, a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler recovers the signal in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity for a broad family of random and deterministic sensing matrices. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give polynomial-time, near-optimal sample complexity guarantees for diffusion-prior sparse recovery, plus total variation bounds for posterior sampling.

entry.title: Playing the SMR Game with Existential Honesty: a study of keeping blockchain consensus safe when no validator is guaranteed honest
entry.summary: Playing the SMR Game with Existential Honesty arXiv · Nov 19, 2026This paper studies state machine replication when every validator is rational or Byzantine and none is honest. It assumes one unidentified, always-online full node is honest, and clients relay certificates to full nodes and wait before confirming transactions. Under this setup, the protocol is always safe for any validator strategy, and the paper tightly characterizes how much transaction censorship a bribing adversary can achieve. ★★★★ Notable: The authors build an always-safe finalization layer for rational-Byzantine validators using certificate relay and an honest full node, and give a tight characterization of censorship.

entry.title: Filling MoE Serving Idle Gaps with Fine-Tuning: A Paper on Using Expert-Parallel Bubbles
entry.summary: Harvesting Expert-Parallel Bubbles for Fine-Tuning arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper observes that in Mixture-of-Experts language models under expert parallelism, uneven token routing leaves lightly loaded GPUs idle, with bubbles still taking 8% to 13% of prefill time after load balancing. It presents BubbleTea, which predicts per-layer bubbles from the router's token assignment and fills them with short fine-tuning chunks that reuse weights already loaded for serving. On three MoE models served on four A100 GPUs, fine-tuning throughput was 1.9 to 6.2 times that of LLMStation, and p90 inference latency stayed within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use expert-parallel bubbles per layer for fine-tuning; they report 1.9–6.2× higher throughput than LLMStation across three MoE models on four A100 GPUs.

entry.title: Analyzing an Unexplored SASS Control-Code Field: Barrier Exemption and Programmable Warp Priority
entry.summary: Dissecting an Unexplored SASS Control-Code Field: Barrier Exemption and Programmable Warp Priority arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies a previously unexplored control-code field in NVIDIA's native GPU instruction set (SASS), which appears frequently in closed-source libraries such as cuBLAS and cuDNN but is never emitted by nvcc for user programs. Using instruction-level microbenchmarks across GPU architectures from Volta to Blackwell, the authors show the field controls two hardware mechanisms: barrier exemption (EXEMPT) and programmable warp priority (START, TILE, END). They also implement a post-compilation binary optimizer that inserts these marks without changing source code or the compiler, achieving speedups of up to 31.9% on representative kernels across six GPUs. ★★★★ Notable: The authors systematically study an unexplored SASS control-code field, identifying barrier exemption and warp priority mechanisms, and report speedups on six GPUs and in llama.cpp and vLLM.

entry.title: PhysResponse: Testing whether video generators respond correctly to physics
entry.summary: PhysResponse: Probing the Physics of Video Generation with Controlled Interventions arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper introduces PhysResponse, a benchmark that checks whether image-to-video models respond correctly to physical parameters such as gravity, friction and initial speed. Evaluating ten models, the authors find that their parameter errors far exceed those of physically correct videos, and they rarely reproduce both outcomes of a critical transition. The authors also build 72,000 simulated videos with controlled parameters, and fine-tuning on them lowers parameter errors and transfers to real videos and an external physics benchmark. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a benchmark measuring physical parameter responsiveness in video generation, evaluating ten image-to-video models and reporting that fine-tuning on 72,000 simulated videos lowers

entry.title: Pose-Robust Few-Shot Vision-Language-Action Models
entry.summary: Towards Pose-Robust Few-Shot Vision-Language-Action Models arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper addresses why robot manipulation policies fail when the camera or robot base moves after training. The proposed WACO framework uses the arm's forward kinematics as a metric calibration target and the static scene as a world anchor to estimate camera and base shifts from one RGB-D frame. It canonicalises inputs to the calibration viewpoint and fine-tunes the unmodified policy. Reported results show higher success under shifts than the standard few-shot recipe and prior viewpoint-robust methods, in simulation and on a UR5e robot. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use forward-kinematics-placed arm and static scene to separate camera and base shifts, introduce LIBERO-PoseShift, and report gains over baselines in simulation and on a UR5e robot.

entry.title: Neural networks that keep convex, semiconvex, and quasiconvex shapes
entry.summary: Structure-Preserving Neural Approximation of Convex, Semiconvex, and Quasiconvex Functions arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper extends input convex neural networks, which enforce convexity through their architecture, to semiconvex, quasiconvex, and convex transformable functions. It establishes an approximation rate for C^{1,1} convex functions under max-affine approximation and shows that max-affine functions have exact bounded-width network representations. It also develops a finite-probe approximation theory for Lipschitz quasiconvex functions with an L^∞ guarantee, and extends the results to smooth activations such as Softplus and ELU. Experiments on PDE-based approximation problems show that the architectures keep global structure without penalty tuning while remaining competitive in accuracy. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend ICNN structure-preserving approximation to semiconvex, quasiconvex, and convex transformable functions, reporting a W^{1,p} minimax rate and an L^∞ guarantee, with PDE experiments v

entry.title: Benchmark testing whether LLMs can solve postdoc-level natural science research problems
entry.summary: Benchmarking LLM abilities on postdoc-level natural science problems arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper introduces STEMBench, a benchmark of twelve research problems in high-energy physics, astrophysics and neuroscience. Each problem is scored by its field's own figure of merit, with two anchors: a baseline submission using no domain knowledge and an expert reference reproducing a published method. Across eight frontier models, the model winning the most individual tasks does not lead in domain averages. In the high-effort comparison, at least one model's mean score exceeds the expert anchor on seven of twelve tasks. The tasks, graders, anchors and harness are released. ★★★★ Notable: The authors score agents on twelve field-specific research tasks using domain figures of merit, anchored by no-knowledge and expert baselines, across eight frontier models.

entry.title: When Shuffling Fails: Recovering Tokens from Obfuscated KV Caches
entry.summary: When Shuffling Fails: Token Recovery from Obfuscated KV Caches arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper examines a shuffled obfuscation scheme for protecting KV caches in LLM serving. It shows that repeated input tokens make outputs indistinguishable, so the effective state space is about b rather than the claimed b! permutations. The authors present Repeat-to-Reveal, an attack that recovers an equivalent denoiser without the defender's secret parameters and can passively recover token multisets within a secret epoch. They evaluate it against KV-Cloak and other defenses. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors show repeated tokens collapse the permutation state space from b! to b, enabling token recovery; the abstract reports experiments on KV-Cloak across nine models and 3,000 prompts.

entry.title: Functional principal component analysis: minimax-optimal rates from sparse to dense sampling
entry.summary: Functional Principal Component Analysis: Minimax Optimality from Sparse to Dense Designs and Beyond arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies functional principal component analysis (FPCA), a dimension-reduction tool for functional data. It derives minimax-optimal rates for covariance and eigenfunction estimation under noisy discrete observations with random designs, covering sampling frequencies from sparse to dense. The authors also apply the results to FPCA-based functional linear regression and show that the resulting estimator attains the minimax-optimal rate. ★★★★ Notable: The authors close an open minimax gap for FPCA under discrete observation, giving optimal rates from sparse to dense designs and a downstream regression application.

entry.title: Training noise-removal models without storing training images
entry.summary: Training Denoising Models of Any Architecture Without Stored Images arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper asks whether a pretrained denoising model can replace the dataset used to train it. It proposes teacher-supervised training, where a student model learns from random initialization by regressing the teacher's velocity on noisy samples drawn along random-step trajectories, so no images need to be stored. Experiments cover 12 teachers from 6 families and 6 datasets. On CIFAR-10, students 4x smaller than the teacher outperform standard training of the same network. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show that diffusion and flow denoisers of any architecture can be trained without stored images via teacher velocity regression, validated across 12 teachers and 6 datasets.

entry.title: WM^MLLM: Turning Multimodal LLMs into Persistent, Editable World Models
entry.summary: WM^MLLM: Turning MLLMs into World Models arXiv · Nov 18, 2026WM^MLLM is presented as the first interactive world model built on multimodal large language models, generating persistent, editable worlds from a single image. The world state is stored as a panorama with a revision history outside the generators, and the MLLMs convert each user request into operations on this state and check each candidate before accepting it. Reported experiments compare it against six world model baselines and 15 CompBench baselines, with results showing higher scores on environment-recovery metrics and more completed camera round trips. The paper also reports that revisits reproduce earlier views and that local edits leave pixels outside their region unchanged. ★★★★ Notable: The authors externalize world state as a revision-tracked panorama that MLLMs read and write, reporting top scores on MBench-A against six baselines and consistency on revisits and local edits.

entry.title: Rare-tail statistics for learning biased Gaussian halfspaces under label noise
entry.summary: Rare-Tail Statistics For Learning Biased Gaussian Halfspaces with Label Noise arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies learning general Gaussian halfspaces when labels are noisy, focusing on cases where the bias is large. It proposes the rare-tail mean estimator, a simple one-shot statistic that averages only the minority-class observations. Under a broad class of label noise models, the estimator recovers the halfspace direction at the information-theoretic sample rate up to log factors, while classical averaging is shown to be suboptimal in this regime. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a simple minority-class mean estimator reported to reach the information-theoretic sample rate for noisy Gaussian halfspaces in the large-bias regime.

entry.title: Convergence speed of the final SGD iterate in convex optimization
entry.summary: Nearly Tight Almost Sure Convergence Rates for the Last iterate of SGD arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies how the error of the last iterate of stochastic (sub)gradient descent converges almost surely for convex objectives. For smooth objectives the error decays at rate k^(-1/3) when a stationary minimizer exists and k^(-1/4) otherwise, up to polylogarithmic factors. The latter rate also holds for nonsmooth convex objectives, using deterministic, anytime stepsize policies. Matching lower bounds show the exponents -1/3 and -1/4 are optimal up to polylogarithmic factors. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give nearly tight almost sure last-iterate SGD rates for smooth and nonsmooth convex objectives, matched by lower bounds.

entry.title: Faster convergence can mean a wrong answer in federated optimization
entry.summary: Faster to the Wrong Answer: The Price of Local Updates in Federated Optimization arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies how local computation on clients in federated optimization can introduce bias, so the fixed point differs from the global minimizer. For strongly convex quadratic objectives with a bounded surrogate condition number, it derives the exact minimum worst-case bias per unit heterogeneity. It shows that local gradient descent with small step sizes and proximal updates attains this bound, reduces arbitrary-dimension cases to scalar curvature distributions, and extends the bound to smooth strongly convex objectives and inexact local solves. ★★★★ Notable: The authors derive an exact worst-case bias bound for local updates under a conditioning constraint and reduce arbitrary-dimension problems to scalar curvatures.

entry.title: Checking Executable Legal Rules Against Real Records: Transitional Provisions and Korean SME Status
entry.summary: Grading Executable Legal Rules Against Independent Records: Transitional Provisions and Korean SME Status arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper introduces LexTemporis, a benchmark that checks programs converting laws into decision rules against records of small and medium enterprise status disclosed by 10,901 Korean listed firm-years, rather than against the author's own reading. An appendix adds comparison cases from US income tax and German hospital minimum volumes. The authors find that one transitional provision raises agreement with the disclosures from 83-86% to 89-90%. They also report that grading against the author's reading can overstate how well legal programs perform. ★★★★ Notable: The authors grade LLM-written legal rules against 10,901 disclosed Korean SME firm-years rather than the author's reading, reporting four-model comparisons.

entry.title: Standard adiabatic quantum optimization may gain a subexponential speedup
entry.summary: Vanilla Adiabatic Quantum Optimization Can Have Subexponential Advantage arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper constructs a family of objective functions for which standard adiabatic quantum optimization, evolving under a given Hamiltonian, finds the global minimizer in polynomial time. In the black-box model, the authors state that any classical algorithm needs exp(n^Ω(1)) time for the same task. The result replaces the linearization technique used in an earlier work by Leng et al., which used a transverse field Ising mixer. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a construction giving subexponential quantum advantage for vanilla adiabatic optimization in the black-box model, replacing the prior linearization technique with a new one.

entry.title: Rethinking contrastive training targets for radiology image-text pretraining
entry.summary: Rethinking Contrastive Targets in Radiology Language-Image Pretraining arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper examines CLIP-style contrastive pretraining on radiology image-report pairs, where only the paired report counts as positive and all other reports in the batch are negatives. The authors argue this target is structurally biased because many unpaired reports share clinical findings with the image, and they build a synthetic testbed, CLEVR-Radiology, that reproduces the resulting failures. They propose CorLIP, which treats any report whose clinical assertions agree with the image as positive, requiring no architecture changes. The method largely removes post-peak degradation, enables stable large-batch training up to batch size 2048, and transfers from chest X-ray to 3D CT. ★★★★ Notable: The authors argue CLIP's paired-identity target is systematically biased in radiology, propose CorLIP, and report gains on a synthetic testbed, chest X-ray, and 3D CT.

entry.title: Optimal deep nonparametric regression with bounded Lipschitz constants: a method for stable neural network predictions under input noise
entry.summary: Optimal Deep Nonparametric Regression with Uniformly Bounded Lipschitz Constants arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper develops a approximation theory for deep ReLU networks under a split spectral norm product constraint, showing that sufficiently smooth Hölder functions can be uniformly approximated as depth increases while the norm-product bound stays fixed. Building on this, the authors propose a penalized least squares estimator whose Lipschitz constant is uniformly bounded yet which attains the optimal nonparametric rate up to a logarithmic factor. The paper also derives optimal prediction rates for two-stage learning and robustness guarantees under adversarial input perturbations. Numerical studies indicate the estimator keeps sensitivity to input perturbations well controlled while its prediction accuracy is comparable to classical deep network methods. ★★★★ Notable: The authors establish approximation theory for deep ReLU networks under a split spectral norm constraint and propose an estimator achieving near-optimal rates with bounded Lipschitz constant.

entry.title: Facet-SLAM: Real-Time Triangle Splatting SLAM
entry.summary: Facet-SLAM: Real-Time Triangle Splatting SLAM arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper presents Facet-SLAM, the first real-time triangle splatting SLAM system for RGB-D cameras. The tracker sets each triangle's centroid from fused depth and registers frames to these centroids using GICP, while the mapper is restricted to non-translating updates. The authors report competitive tracking accuracy at about 100 FPS on a desktop GPU and sensor-rate operation on a Jetson AGX Orin. Compared with photometric tracking, it is over 20 times faster with matched rendering quality, and on Replica it reduces the Delaunay mesh chamfer distance from 1.55 cm to 0.86 cm. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present a real-time triangle splatting SLAM for RGB-D, reporting over 20x speedup and Chamfer distance reduced from 1.55 to 0.86 cm on Replica.

entry.title: Heart MRI-informed ECG for biologically grounded cardiomyopathy detection
entry.summary: Cardiac MRI-informed electrocardiography enables biologically grounded cardiomyopathy detection arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper presents MyoECG, a framework that transfers myocardial structural and functional knowledge from cardiac MRI into standard 12-lead ECGs, enabling cardiomyopathy detection and subtype classification from ECGs alone. It was validated on over 1.8 million ECGs from seven independent datasets, with AUROCs of 0.800 to 0.974 for cardiomyopathy detection. In a multi-reader study, MyoECG assistance improved six cardiologists' sensitivity and specificity. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors propose cross-modal distillation from CMR into 12-lead ECG, reporting AUROCs of 0.800-0.974 across seven independent datasets and improved reader sensitivity and specificity.

entry.title: Vanguard: Deciding When a Small Model's Draft Can Be Trusted in Vision-Language Agents
entry.summary: Vanguard: Knowing When to Trust the Draft in Speculative Vision-Language Agents arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper presents Vanguard, a training-free judge for speculative step generation in vision-language agents. A small model drafts each action, and a general decision model that can see the screenshot assigns each candidate a probability of being correct; the draft is kept if it clears a threshold, otherwise the large model writes the step. The authors report that on web, mobile and embodied agent tasks, a 2B draft judged by Vanguard is at least as accurate as its 8B target, while the target writes only a minority of steps. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a training-free, screenshot-aware judge letting small drafts beat large targets; the authors report results on Mind2Web, EB-ALFRED, and mobile and web agent tasks.

entry.title: MLE Agents: Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering for Large-Scale Recommendation Systems
entry.summary: MLE Agents: Autonomous ML Engineering in Large-scale Recommendation Systems arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper presents human-on-the-loop machine learning engineer (MLE) agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes on large-scale search rankers, while engineers keep control over objective design, search direction, and final review. In one campaign, the system completed 1,097 candidate experiments and accepted 325, a 29.6% acceptance rate. Its best model increased search volume by 0.23% in a large-scale A/B test. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply autonomous LLM agents to industry-scale search ranking, addressing slow feedback and offline-online mismatch; they report 1,097 experiments, 325 accepted, and a 0.23% search-volume g

entry.title: Infinity-Wasserstein Robust PCA: Exact Reformulation, Sample Guarantee, and Fast Algorithm
entry.summary: Infinity-Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Principal Component Analysis: Exact Reformulation, Finite-Sample Guarantee, and Efficient Algorithm arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies principal component analysis under distributional uncertainty by building a distributionally robust version based on the infinity-Wasserstein distance. The authors derive an exact finite-dimensional reformulation of this model and identify a worst-case distribution that attains the inner maximum. Assuming the true distribution has a finite fourth moment, they prove a uniform finite-sample performance guarantee. An iteratively reweighted majorization-minimization algorithm is developed for the resulting nonconvex, nonsmooth problem, and numerical experiments show its efficiency and practical effectiveness. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply infinity-Wasserstein DRO to PCA, deriving an exact finite-dimensional reformulation, a worst-case distribution, a finite-sample guarantee, and experiments on efficiency and downstrea

entry.title: MobileWeave: Program-First Task Synthesis for Training Mobile GUI Agents
entry.summary: MobileWeave: Program-First Synthesis of Dependency-Linked Tasks for Training Mobile GUI Agents arXiv · Nov 18, 2026MobileWeave synthesizes each training task as an executable program built from a simulator's app implementations, linking subtasks through explicit value and object dependencies. Single- and cross-app composite programs are verified by native execution, and their instructions and completion checks are derived from the same program. Training with teacher trajectories and recovery supervision, MobileWeave-8B improves on its base model by 26.7 points on MobileGym and by 8.6, 21.3, and 17.6 points on AndroidWorld, AndroidLab, and MobileWorld. ★★★★ Notable: The authors synthesize mobile GUI tasks as dependency-linked executable programs, reporting gains on several benchmarks and releasing data, model, and code.

entry.title: RoboBuilder: AI Agents Co-Designing Robots with Real-World Video Feedback
entry.summary: RoboBuilder: Agentic Robot Co-Design with Real-world Video Feedback in the Loop arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper introduces RoboBuilder, a benchmark where coding agents co-design a robot's hardware and program from standard parts and one custom 3D-printed part. Designs that pass in simulation are built and tested on a physical course, and agents refine their simulator using measurements they request and videos of real runs. The agents solved nearly all easy obstacles but struggled at harder levels and in the real world, where 66% of simulated passes held. After viewing video of a real failure, agents redesigned their robots and removed 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present a closed-loop benchmark where coding agents co-design robot hardware and programs using real-world video feedback. The abstract reports 16,427 simulations and 135 physical robots,

entry.title: A fast, programmable GPU-to-CPU call layer for GPU-initiated communication
entry.summary: A Fast, Programmable GPU-to-CPU Invocation Layer for GPU-Initiated Communication arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper presents KIWI, a programmable reverse-offload framework in which GPU kernels hand communication operations to host-side proxy threads instead of GPU threads controlling transport. The authors report sub-microsecond one-way device-to-host latency and hundreds of millions of operations per second. KIWI-P2P, a SHMEM-like library built on it, outperforms existing GPUDirect Async implementations in latency and bandwidth, while KIWI-EP reduces expert-parallel communication latency on AMD GPUs and time per output token in vLLM. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors propose reverse offload as a first-class, programmable communication path, reporting up to 2.3x lower expert-parallel latency on AMD GPUs.

entry.title: Plug-and-play watermarking that traces leaked Mixture-of-Experts LLM copies to individual licensees
entry.summary: Plug-and-Play Multi-Licensee Robust Watermarking for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper presents PPMoE, the first plug-and-play watermarking framework for Mixture-of-Experts large language models that supports multiple licensees. It trains compact, mergeable weight modules that steer the MoE router toward distinct, compatible routing patterns, so licensee-specific watermarks can be embedded at distribution time without retraining. The authors report high attribution accuracy under white-box and black-box threat models, with base model utility preserved and robustness against adaptive removal attacks across five MoE models and seven datasets. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose mergeable incremental modules steering MoE routers for multi-licensee watermarking, reporting validation on five MoE models and seven datasets under white- and black-box attributio

entry.title: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Clinical Discovery
entry.summary: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery from Clinical Data arXiv · Nov 6, 2026This paper presents Glyph, a framework that uses foundation models and sparse autoencoders to extract features from multimodal, unstructured clinical data, interprets them as coded clinical concepts, and evaluates their value for scientific discovery. Applied to abdominal CT volumes, CT radiology reports, and lab measurements from 41,628 patients, it identified 397 predictive concepts supported by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations. Most associations were reproducible in held-out cohorts across different sites. ★★★★ Notable: The authors interpret foundation-model latent features as clinical concepts, reporting 397 predictive concepts and 4,463 significant associations across 41,628 patients.

entry.title: Four Ciphers in One: Full-Round Attacks on the LLBC Reference Implementation
entry.summary: Four Ciphers in One: Full-Round Attacks on the Reference Implementation of LLBC IACR ePrint · Nov 15, 2026LLBC is a 128-bit low-latency block cipher for IoT, proposed in 2025. This paper finds that its released reference implementation differs from the published specification in eight points, including rotation amounts. The authors show the implementation splits into four independent 32-bit ciphers and attack all 20 rounds, decrypting on a single PC in 175.5 seconds. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors show the reference implementation deviates from the specification, splits into independent ciphers, and report full 20-round attacks.

entry.title: Error bounds for Falcon's fast Fourier sampler under fixed-point arithmetic
entry.summary: Bounds of Falcon's Fast Fourier Sampler with Fixed-Point Arithmetic IACR ePrint · Nov 16, 2026This paper bounds the Rényi divergence between Falcon's fast Fourier sampler in real arithmetic and its fixed-point implementation, on the tail-cut event. It gives resulting security bit levels for n=512 at λ=128 and n=1024 at λ=256 over 2^64 signatures. The authors propose four changes to the fixed-point implementation, with proofs partly machine-checked in CryptoLine and Lean. ★★★★ Notable: The authors bound Rényi divergence for Falcon's fixed-point sampler and propose four implementation changes, backed by machine-checked proofs and three code-alignment hypotheses.

entry.title: Fair Splitting of Goods and Chores Over Time
entry.summary: Temporal Fair Division: Simultaneous Guarantees for Goods and Chores arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies fair division of indivisible goods and chores when items arrive one at a time and must be assigned immediately and irrevocably. For goods, it gives a polynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact temporal proportionality up to one item, a 1/n approximation to temporal maximin share, and a 1/(n-1) approximation to temporal envy-freeness up to one item. For chores, it gives an algorithm achieving exact TPROP1 and a 2-1/n approximation to temporal maximin share, and shows this factor is optimal under that constraint. ★★★★ Notable: The authors study temporal fair division of indivisible goods and chores, reporting polynomial-time algorithms that simultaneously achieve TPROP1, TMMS and TEF1 approximations, plus tight-bound and im

entry.title: Singlet flags restore circuit distance of shuttled quantum LDPC codes in silicon
entry.summary: Singlet flags: using native entanglement to restore the circuit distance of shuttled qLDPC codes in silicon arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper addresses measuring high-weight checks of quantum LDPC codes on silicon spin-qubit processors by shuttling an ancilla electron. The authors make the ancilla half of a spin singlet whose partner stays home, and use a Bell measurement at the end of each check as a flag for isolated bit-flip faults during the walk. Tests on new distance-6 codes and circuit-level simulations show that the flag restores circuit distance and lowers logical error rates across several code families. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use a spin-singlet partner as a flag to restore circuit distance of shuttled qLDPC codes, with exact distance solvers and circuit-level simulations reported.

entry.title: QCCDCert: A formally verified compiler for co-designing QCCD trapped-ion quantum hardware and software
entry.summary: QCCDCert: Formally Verified Compilation for QCCD Co-Design arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper presents a co-design framework built on a compiler verified in the Lean language, for comparing trapped-ion QCCD quantum computers with different trap sizes and layouts. Hardware descriptions and operating rules are treated as compiler inputs, so one theorem covers every candidate design. On 75 benchmark programs of 11 to 130 qubits, the best design found reduced modeled execution time by 66% on average compared with the worst design of equal capacity. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply a Lean-verified compiler to QCCD co-design, proving one theorem across designs. They report 75 benchmarks and 11 defects in three prior compilers.

entry.title: Scrambling as the source of entanglement cost in non-local quantum computation
entry.summary: Scrambling leads to entanglement cost in NLQC arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies the entanglement needed to implement a joint quantum channel in non-local quantum computation (NLQC). The authors introduce a new lower-bound technique based on scrambling, showing that a unitary has zero entanglement cost exactly when it does not scramble. They further show that the tripartite mutual information, which measures scrambling, gives a quantitative lower bound on NLQC entanglement cost. Using this bound, they also prove that controllable correlation is a faithful lower bound, resolving a conjecture of Cleve and May. ★★★★ Notable: The authors link scrambling to NLQC entanglement cost, give a faithful lower bound, and report resolving a Cleve-May conjecture.

entry.title: Covering Pauli Observables: Sampling Thresholds and Design Effect of Measurement Settings
entry.summary: Covering the Pauli Observables: Sampling Thresholds and the Design Effect of a Measurement Setting arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper studies how many random measurement settings are needed to cover a given fraction of all Pauli observables, where each setting assigns X, Y, or Z to every qubit and one run estimates all observables it covers. It shows that the covered fraction has a sharp threshold at a growth rate of 3^(3/4) per qubit and gives an explicit expression for the number of settings needed, with random sampling asymptotically optimal up to a factor below 1.69. The authors also define a design effect for each setting that captures correlations among estimates, and in six-qubit simulations report 7.6 to 38 times fewer circuit runs than measuring observables independently. ★★★★ Notable: The authors link Pauli observable covering to rate-distortion theory, giving a 3^{3/4} threshold and near-optimal random sampling, plus a closed-form mean design effect verified in six-qubit simulatio

entry.title: Stephen: Verifying Sequencer-Aided Coordination Systems with Cross-View Prophecy
entry.summary: Stephen: Verifying Sequencer-Aided Coordination Systems with Cross-View Prophecy arXiv · Nov 18, 2026Many distributed systems use dedicated sequencers to order requests, with replicas committing them in that order. This paper presents Stephen, a framework that extends prophecy variables across view changes so a proof can follow each request until it is committed or permanently discarded. The authors found and fixed bugs in existing implementations, including one that could lose committed requests. Applied to NOPaxos, Corfu and LazyLog, the framework yields verified implementations with machine-checked linearizability proofs that perform within 17% of unverified open-source versions. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose cross-view prophecy variables for sequencer view changes, find and fix a bug losing committed requests, and report machine-checked linearizability proofs for NOPaxos, Corfu, and La

entry.title: Sightline: Faster Vector Graphics Generation via Long-Window Speculative Decoding
entry.summary: Sightline: Long-Window Speculative Decoding for Fast SVG Generation arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper speeds up models that generate Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) code one token at a time, without changing their outputs. The proposed method, Sightline, pairs a verification window as long as the drafter's horizon with a draft tree wide enough to fill it. Across text-to-SVG and image-to-SVG benchmarks, it was the fastest of the compared lossless decoders in every setting. ★★★★ Notable: The authors match verification window to drafter horizon with wide draft trees, reporting fastest lossless decoding across six SVG benchmarks.

entry.title: When Accuracy Hides Risk: Risk-Controlled Confirmation of Surgical Safety Views
entry.summary: When accuracy hides risk: risk-controlled confirmation of the critical view of safety under expert disagreement arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies automated confirmation of the critical view of safety (CVS) in laparoscopic cholecystectomy, showing that standard threshold calibration concentrates false confirmations on videos where expert raters disagree. The authors propose certified confirmation, a risk-controlled rule that selects its threshold through multiple testing to limit false confirmations. In a pre-specified evaluation on 300 test videos from the SAGES CVS Challenge, it substantially reduced false confirmations of disputed videos compared with standard calibration. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show standard threshold calibration concentrates false confirmations on disputed videos and propose a risk-controlled rule, reported on the SAGES CVS Challenge test set.

entry.title: Individually addressable CCZ gates on near-good quantum LDPC codes, and near-optimal magic state protocols
entry.summary: Addressable transversal CCZ gates on almost good quantum LDPC codes and nearly optimal magic state protocols arXiv · Nov 18, 2026Under a uniform subfield product expansion assumption, the paper constructs quantum LDPC codes with distance Ω_ε(N/log²N) that support at least N^{1-ε} individually addressable logical CCZ gates. The codes are built as balanced products of expanding graph covers. Applications include CCZ distillation with arbitrarily small overhead exponent and a magic state fountain that prepares many encoded CCZ states. ★★★★ Notable: The authors construct qLDPC codes with addressable transversal CCZ gates and near-optimal magic state protocols, relying on a subfield product expansion assumption, reporting distance and gate-count b

entry.title: Separating QMA from QCMA via a classical oracle and a polynomial switching lemma
entry.summary: Separating QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy via a Switching Lemma for Polynomials arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper constructs a classical oracle relative to which QMA is not contained in the QCMA hierarchy. Its main tool is a switching lemma for bounded polynomials, whose parameters do not depend on the number of input variables. The authors also build two further oracles: one where QCMA collapses to P but QMA does not, and one where QMA collapses to P but PP does not. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a polynomial switching lemma giving a new viewpoint on a QMA versus QCMA oracle separation, plus two further collapse separations.

entry.title: Gradient averaging makes sketched Newton methods statistically efficient.
entry.summary: A Free Lunch: Gradient Averaging Achieves Optimal Statistical Efficiency in Newton Sketch arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies statistical inference for online sketched Newton methods, where each Newton system is approximately solved by an inner randomized sketching solver to reduce computational cost. The authors show that replacing the stochastic gradient with a moving average at each step reduces the extra covariance caused by sketching, without requiring additional oracle evaluations. They prove that the averaged iterate attains the minimax optimal limiting covariance, matching the exact Newton method. Numerical experiments on linear and logistic regression support the theoretical covariance comparisons. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show gradient averaging removes the statistical cost of Newton sketch, with the averaged iterate reaching minimax-optimal covariance; numerical experiments on linear and logistic regressio

entry.title: Rented Oscillations: Attacks and Defenses for Synchronized Workloads in Shared Data Centers
entry.summary: Rented Oscillations: Multi-Tenant Data Center Workload Synchronization Attacks and Mitigation arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies a stealthy attacker who rents computing capacity in a multi-tenant data center and runs deliberately unoptimized large language model training, synchronizing many workloads into large periodic power oscillations. Each workload remains individually hard to distinguish from benign training. The authors characterize the periodicity experimentally, use a hardware-grounded threat model supported by supercomputer experiments, and identify oscillatory weak points in the network. They propose signal-energy-based detection and a mitigation that re-times workloads to reduce oscillatory energy, validated with power hardware-in-the-loop experiments and real-time simulations on a surrogate model of the Saudi Arabian transmission network. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a stealthy attack synchronizing rented data center workloads into periodic oscillations, with detection and re-timing mitigation validated on PHIL experiments and a Saudi grid surro

entry.title: Same model, different results: numerical execution and fairness audit reproducibility
entry.summary: Same Model, Different People: Numerical Execution Contracts and the Reproducibility of Fairness Audits arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper argues that fairness audits treat a trained model as a fixed decision function, yet the arithmetic used to evaluate it also affects outcomes. Holding the model, data, threshold and audit code fixed, the authors vary the numerical execution settings across several models and public tasks. Reduced-precision deployment configurations changed some decisions and diagnostic verdicts, so the audit result depends on the configuration, and the paper proposes an audit stability protocol. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors treat numerical execution contracts as part of fairness audits, testing arithmetic causally in two tiers across four public tasks, models and hardware, and propose an audit stability proto

entry.title: What interpolators store versus what they express: an information-theoretic framework for benign overfitting and label-free model selection
entry.summary: What Interpolators Store and What They Express: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Benign Overfitting and Label-Free Model Selection arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper proposes an information-theoretic framework that separates what an interpolating learner stores about its training labels from what it expresses about the sample in its predictions at new inputs. It shows every interpolator stores the same amount of label-noise information, so storage cannot distinguish interpolators, while expressed information V bounds excess risk and explains benign overfitting as vanishing expression. V also yields a model-selection criterion that requires no held-out labels, and on 15 noisy datasets it outperformed holdout validation and conditional mutual information selection. ★★★★ Notable: The authors separate storage from expression, bound excess risk by expressed information V, and report a label-free selection criterion tested on 15 noisy datasets.

entry.title: How Uncertain Is My Action? Self-Correcting Visual Planning with Frozen World Models
entry.summary: How Uncertain Is My Action? Self-Correcting Visual Planning with Frozen World Models arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper addresses visual planning with a frozen latent world model and sampling-based model predictive control, where the executed action can differ from the commanded one without the model noticing. The authors run the model in reverse, predicting what should be observed under a hypothesized actuation shift and comparing that with actual observations to detect and estimate the shift. Experiments on PushT, TwoRoom, OGBench-Cube and a real robotic arm report improved success rates and reduced reach error after self-correction. ★★★★ Notable: The authors run a frozen world model in reverse to detect and estimate action shifts, with a locally optimal test and Cramér-Rao error bars. The paper reports validation on PushT, TwoRoom, OGBench-Cub

entry.title: Error buildup in diffusion sampling with imperfect learned scores
entry.summary: Error accumulation in reverse diffusion with an imperfect score: beyond path-space analyses arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper studies how errors in learned score functions accumulate when generating samples through reverse diffusion. Prior analyses bound this sampling error in total variation, with error growing polynomially over the process horizon. The authors show that avoiding path-space analysis can mitigate this accumulation when the target distribution satisfies a Poincaré inequality, and they extend the framework to a weaker error metric for general distributions. They also show that the diffusion sampler nearly achieves optimal total variation error for a given Poincaré constant bound. ★★★★ Notable: The authors avoid path-space analysis to mitigate error accumulation under a Poincaré inequality, and report near-optimal total variation error via theory.

entry.title: Efficient Variance-Aware Reinforcement Learning in Time-Inhomogeneous Linear MDPs
entry.summary: Efficient Variance-Aware Reinforcement Learning in Time-Inhomogeneous Linear MDPs arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies variance-dependent reinforcement learning in episodic time-inhomogeneous linear Markov decision processes. It proposes VA-LSVI-UCB++, a computationally efficient algorithm with a regret bound that adapts to the smaller of two realized trajectory variances. In deterministic environments, the bound has no polynomial dependence on the number of episodes K. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose VA-LSVI-UCB++, attaining variance-dependent regret in linear MDPs that removes polynomial-in-K terms in deterministic environments.

entry.title: DOCK: A Self-Supervised Object-Centric Representation for Robot Planning, Grounded in Kinematics
entry.summary: DOCK: Dual-Stream-Inspired Self-Supervised Object-Centric Representations Grounded in Robot Kinematics arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper finds that in latent-space planners, the distance between frozen DINO and V-JEPA features barely tracks how far an object is from its goal. The authors propose DOCK, which learns an object representation from forward kinematics of joint angles on grasped objects, without annotation.
