Trained on about 404K displacement pairs from simulated kitchen scenes, it places the object in 15 of 21 tasks when used as a planning cost, matching an oracle that reads the true object position. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use forward kinematics on joint angles as an annotation-free proxy for object displacement, learning object representations that match physical motion; reported on 21 simulated kitchen pla

entry.title: Hidden-structure graph models: when counting small motifs cannot tell configurations apart
entry.summary: Bounded-Order Non-Identifiability in Latent Structure Block Models: The Fiber in Closed Form arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies how much information is lost when a graph is summarized by counts of finitely many small subgraphs (motifs) rather than all of them. It focuses on latent structure block models with positions on K rays, equivalent to rank-two degree-corrected block models. The authors give a closed-form description of the one-dimensional family of configurations that agree on all graphs with fewer than 2K-1 vertices. They show the friendship graph F_{K-1} is its unique edge-minimal separator, so no single fixed motif order works for every K. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a closed-form non-identifiability fiber for bounded-order motif truncation, sharpening prior results; the abstract reports bounds at K=4 and spectral-method experiments.

entry.title: Dreaming Up Authors: How Often LLMs Invent Paper Authors, and Why Rarely Cited Papers Are Affected More
entry.summary: Dreaming Up Authors: Factual Prevalence and LLM Hallucinations in Academic Authorship Attribution arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies why large language models hallucinate when asked who wrote academic papers, focusing on how common a fact is in training data. The authors use citation count as a proxy for factual prevalence and build a dataset of 1.92 million papers across eight disciplines. Experiments on three LLMs show hallucination rates fall as citation counts rise, exceeding 98% for rarely cited papers and dropping below 37% for highly cited ones. The authors also report that failures mainly reflect retrieval limitations rather than missing knowledge, and that prevalence is encoded in model representations before generation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use citation count as a proxy for factual prevalence, reporting an inverse hallucination relationship across 1.92M papers, three LLMs, and hidden-state probing.

entry.title: ORGANIC3D: Anchoring 3D CT Vision-Language Models to Organ-Level Anatomical Evidence
entry.summary: ORGANIC3D: Grounding 3D CT Vision Language Models in Organ Level Image Text Coupling arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper introduces ORGANIC3D, a framework for checking whether 3D CT vision-language models base their predictions on the correct anatomical evidence and for improving alignment between organs and text. The authors evaluate models using controlled interventions such as organ erasure, lesion replacement, and laterality perturbation, and train on edited scans. They report state-of-the-art classification AUROC on CTRATE, Merlin, and RADChestCT, along with 77% laterality accuracy. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose organ-level image-text alignment evaluation via organ erasure and laterality interventions, reporting SOTA AUROC on CTRATE, Merlin, and RADChestCT.

entry.title: ACaM: Automated capability modeling to find hidden dangers in AI agent tools
entry.summary: ACaM: Automated Capability Modeling for Agentic AI Security arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper addresses agentic AI systems, where tools can hide dangerous behavior that their natural-language descriptions do not mention, a gap it calls Description-Code Inconsistency. It proposes ACaM, a neurosymbolic method that derives each tool's capabilities from its code using static analysis, compiling agent source code into a capability property graph to reconstruct threat chains across multiple tool calls. Evaluated on 43 real-world agents, ACaM reports 98.3% macro-F1 on capability properties for 24 annotated agents and discovers hundreds of structural vulnerabilities, ten confirmed with proof-of-concept exploits. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors propose code-grounded capability modeling against description-code inconsistency, evaluated on 43 real agents with ten confirmed proof-of-concept exploits.

entry.title: Compute Before Digitizing: ADC-less Mixed-Signal Readout for Cryogenic Qubits
entry.summary: Compute Before You Digitize: ADC-less Mixed-Signal Processing for Scalable Cryogenic Qubit Readout arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper presents DIRAC, an in-cryostat qubit readout architecture that removes Nyquist-rate analog-to-digital converters by performing demodulation and averaging in the analog domain. Passive complex mixers, ping-pong active-RC integrators, and a time-domain digitizing stage process the front-end output before conversion. Designed in 22 nm FD-SOI and evaluated at 4 K on 1.12M experimental shots, it matches the fidelity of an FP32 digital pipeline while using far less energy. It also reduces 4 K power per physical qubit by 50.4% relative to a fixed-point pipeline. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose ADC-less cryogenic qubit readout using analog computation; they report FP32-matching fidelity on 1.12M shots and energy and logical-error comparisons.

entry.title: LIC-Audit: Are Reported Gains in Learned Image Compression Comparable?
entry.summary: LIC-Audit: How Comparable Are Reported Gains in Learned Image Compression? arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper audits performance claims in learned image compression, analyzing 353 rate-distortion curves and 28,193 encode-decode records from eight public codec releases. It finds that different VTM reference versions, inconsistent conventions for counting bits, computing PSNR, and padding images, and per-image variation all affect whether small gains are comparable or statistically significant. The authors also provide a versioned evaluation protocol, a leaderboard, benchmark data, and reporting guidelines. ★★★★ Notable: The authors audit BD-rate comparability in learned image compression, report 353 curves and 28,193 encode-decode records, and propose a versioned evaluation protocol affecting this subfield's reportin

entry.title: Which tokens, in what order, and how fast? Theory of on-policy distillation objectives
entry.summary: Which Tokens, in What Order, and How Fast? A Theoretical Analysis of On-Policy Distillation Objectives arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper theoretically analyzes how the choice of on-policy distillation (OPD) objective determines which tokens are prioritized, the order of learning, and learning efficiency. It finds that sequence-level OPD has a future agreement bias, causing later token positions to match the teacher first while earlier positions may favor tokens the teacher considers improbable. The authors prove that forward KL gives a well-behaved optimization landscape, whereas other f-divergences such as reverse KL can suffer vanishing gradients even when student and teacher are far apart. ★★★★ Notable: The authors analyze sequence-level versus token-level on-policy distillation, revealing future agreement bias and reverse learning order, and prove divergence choice affects gradient optimization.

entry.title: Optimal joint bounds for estimating and preparing sparse quantum ground states
entry.summary: Optimal Joint Bounds for Sparse Ground-State Energy Estimation and Ground-State Preparation arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper studies the quantum query complexity of ground-state energy estimation and ground-state preparation for sparse Hamiltonians. It proves lower bounds that scale with the square root of the sparsity, the overlap, the error, and the gap, even for stoquastic Hamiltonians. The authors also provide matching upper-bound algorithms in a reversible in-place sparse-location model. These results show that the square-root dependence on sparsity is both necessary and sufficient. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give matching sparse-query lower and upper bounds for GSEE and GSP, jointly in sparsity s, overlap, precision and failure probability.

entry.title: Using formal Vlasov-Maxwell proofs to check plasma simulation results
entry.summary: Reusing formal Vlasov-Maxwell proofs to certify plasma solver outputs arXiv · Nov 15, 2026This paper reuses a theorem from OpenAI's Lean 4 relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell library, stating that initial fields determine the field at an outside point until plasma signals reach it, and bounding energy leaving a surrounding box before signals arrive. The authors add new Lean proofs and numerical bounds that serve as particle-free references for particle-in-cell simulations across three tasks. They use these to expose boundary and initialization errors in WarpX and Smilei. ★★★★ Notable: The authors reuse a Lean-formalized Vlasov-Maxwell theorem to derive particle-free PIC references, reporting checks on three tasks and on WarpX and Smilei that exposed errors.

entry.title: Ephyra: A Property-Based Testing Framework for the LLM Era
entry.summary: Ephyra: A Property-Based Testing Framework for the LLM Era arXiv · Oct 24, 2026This paper presents Ephyra, a Rust property-based testing library built on customizability, observability, and generator synthesis. Users can compose their own testing loops from generation, mutation, and shrinking, and synthesize these components to satisfy functional predicates. Applied to 14 open source systems, it found 349 bugs, of which 300 were reported, across databases, a policy engine, an SQL prover, a URL parser, Rust reimplementations of tools, and compilers. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present a Rust PBT library with customizable loops and generator synthesis, reporting 349 bugs found across 14 open source systems.

entry.title: Passable for whom? Personalizing sidewalk accessibility judgments from a few answers
entry.summary: Passable for Whom? Few-Shot Learning for Personal Calibration of Sidewalk Accessibility Perception for Human-Centered Autonomous Driving arXiv · Nov 15, 2026This paper studies whether a sidewalk is passable depends on the individual, since people using the same mobility aid can disagree about the same image. The authors propose PassCal, which predicts a new person's judgments of unseen sidewalk scenes from a few of their answers, separating a shared scene description from the person's interpretation. It was evaluated on 8,883 judgments from 135 mobility-aid users rating 50 scenes. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose few-shot personal calibration of sidewalk passability, reporting Brier improvement from 0.550 to 0.479 with eight answers across 135 users.

entry.title: Restoring Robustness in Quantized Robot Policies by Correcting Vulnerable States
entry.summary: Think Before You Distill: Generalization Recovery in Quantized VLAs via Selective Policy Distillation arXiv · Oct 5, 2026This paper studies whether post-training quantization of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) robot policies preserves robustness and generalization under environmental disturbances, not just in-distribution performance. The authors find quantized policies become fragile to subtle variations, with action discrepancies concentrated in a small set of states. They propose PIVOT-Q, an on-policy distillation method that uses the full-precision model as teacher and corrects only vulnerable states. Across seven LIBERO-Plus variations, PIVOT-Q recovers performance and outperforms full-state distillation while using 7.4% of its budget. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes PIVOT-Q, selectively distilling vulnerable states of quantized VLAs under perturbations; the authors report it beats full-state distillation across seven LIBERO-Plus perturbations and multipl

entry.title: NVIDIA Kumo Tabular: a family of open AI models for predicting outcomes from spreadsheet-style tables
entry.summary: NVIDIA Kumo Tabular: Pushing the Accuracy-Efficiency Frontier for Tabular Prediction arXiv · Nov 18, 2026Kumo Tabular is a set of open foundation models for classification and regression on tables, in three sizes from 27M to 214M parameters. They are pretrained only on artificial tables and make predictions on new tables without further training. The largest model ranks first on eight benchmarks, and its accuracy improves with model size. It also predicts faster than the runners-up on TabArena and BeyondArena. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce architectural changes for tabular foundation models, report first place on eight benchmarks, and show accuracy gains with model size.

entry.title: A Little Advice Suffices: Diffie-Hellman Is as Hard as Discrete Log
entry.summary: A Little Advice Suffices: Diffie-Hellman Is as Hard as Discrete Logarithm arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper asks whether computing a Diffie-Hellman key is as hard as computing a discrete logarithm. Maurer's earlier reduction worked only under an assumption about short intervals containing enough integers with small prime factors, which had been unproven for thirty years. The authors use a now-known zero-free half-plane for the Riemann zeta function to prove this assumption, removing the condition. They conclude that for every prime p there is an O(log p)-bit advice string, depending only on p, that lets a Diffie-Hellman oracle compute discrete logarithms in any group of order p in polynomial time. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors drop Maurer's thirty-year smooth-interval condition using zero-free-region bounds on smooth integers, and report applications to related impossibility results and Wolf's characterisation.

entry.title: Must You See Fakes to Catch Fakes? Language Points to What to Look For, Real Images to What to Ignore
entry.summary: Must You See Fakes to Catch Fakes? Language Says What to Look For, Real Images What to Ignore arXiv · Nov 17, 2026The paper proposes SaySee, a training-free detector for AI-generated images. It builds a generation direction from paired text descriptions that differ only in authenticity and scores images by projecting their embeddings onto it, then uses real images to correct score offsets caused by format, image type and content. On 24 evaluation sets, SaySee with MoE-ViE reaches a mean AUC of 98.2%, outperforming the best existing detector. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a training-free detector using text-derived generation directions plus real-image offset correction, reporting 98.2% mean AUC over 24 evaluation sets, 4.2 points above the best pri

entry.title: Expressive power of two-dimensional Gaussian fermion tensor network states
entry.summary: Expressivity of two-dimensional Gaussian fermion tensor network states arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies exact tensor network representations of two-dimensional translation-invariant Gaussian fermionic states, covering single-band BCS superconductors and half-filled two-band insulators (including semimetals). For both families, the authors prove that an area law for the Renyi-0 entropy is equivalent to the existence of an exact Gaussian fermionic tensor network state with a finite bond dimension set by that entropy. The paper also gives equivalent characterizations based on compactly supported Wannier-type orbitals and the momentum-space wavefunction. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove that a Rényi-0 area law is equivalent to an exact Gaussian fermionic tensor network representation with finite bond dimension in 2D.

entry.title: A mathematical proof that certain electron-photon ground-state quantities determine the external potentials
entry.summary: Unique continuation for the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper proves a unique continuation property for eigenstates of the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian, viewed as functions of electron configuration with values in spin-photon space. The vector potential may lie in L^6 locally, and the divergence, curl and scalar potential in L^p locally for some p>2. As an application, it proves a Hohenberg-Kohn theorem at positive coupling strength: the spin-summed ground-state density and combined current density determine the external potentials up to a gauge transformation and an additive constant. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove unique continuation for Pauli-Fierz eigenstates under weak regularity and derive a Hohenberg-Kohn theorem at positive coupling.

entry.title: Entanglement cost and classical capacity of multimode Gaussian states and channels
entry.summary: Entanglement cost and classical capacity of multimode Gaussian states and channels arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper studies the entanglement cost and classical capacity of multimode Gaussian states and channels in continuous-variable quantum information. The authors prove that entanglement of formation, Gaussian entanglement of formation, and entanglement cost coincide for finite-energy bipartite Gaussian states, and that this value lower-bounds these quantities for non-Gaussian states with the same covariance matrix. They determine the entanglement cost and the energy-constrained classical capacity of every multimode Gaussian channel, both reducing to Gaussian covariance optimizations. The capacity is achieved by pure Gaussian signals with Gaussian displacement modulation. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove equality of three entanglement measures for Gaussian states and determine multimode Gaussian channel capacity and entanglement cost via proofs.

entry.title: Catalytic imaginarity transformations: using an unconsumed auxiliary system to make otherwise impossible quantum state conversions possible with real operations
entry.summary: Catalytic imaginarity transformations arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper studies catalytic state transformations in the resource theory of imaginarity, a property of quantum states. A catalyst with imaginarity enables conversions that are impossible using only real operations, without being consumed. The authors analyze deterministic conversion, stochastic-approximate conversion, and the effects of catalyst recovery and multiple rounds on the success probability. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show a maximally imaginary pure state is the unique deterministic catalyst and derive optimal stochastic-approximate catalytic success probabilities and tradeoffs, limited to imaginarity t

entry.title: Proving LABS optimality with a quantum-classical branch and bound method
entry.summary: Proven optimality for LABS with quantum-classical branch and bound arXiv · Nov 17, 2026Low autocorrelation binary sequences (LABS) are used as radar phase codes and digital communication sync words. The paper presents a quantum-classical branch and bound algorithm in which fixed-angle QAOA samples the Hamiltonians of search-tree nodes to supply candidate sequences and branching choices, while classical bounds prune the tree. The method either proves optimality or, if stopped early, returns the best sequence found with a certified lower bound and gap. The authors report proven optima for lengths 2 to 30 and explicitly claim no speedup. ★★★★ Notable: The authors embed fixed-angle QAOA in branch and bound to prove LABS optimality, reporting proven optima for lengths 2 to 30 and bound trajectories over time, without claiming speedup.

entry.title: Minimum Measurement Rounds for Perfect Encoded Fusion
entry.summary: Optimal Measurement Rounds for Perfect Encoded Fusion arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper studies encoded fusion, where probabilistic physical fusions implement a logical Bell measurement, and determines the minimum worst-case number of measurement rounds needed to perfectly fuse two blocks of an irreducible [[n,1]] stabilizer code. In a lossless model, the optimum equals the minimum root eccentricity over the local complementation orbit of graphs representing the code, and the lower bound holds for any adaptive perfect strategy. The paper also gives a matching strategy and characterizes the batch sequences possible on all-failure branches via a graph adjacency condition. ★★★★ Notable: The authors determine the optimal worst-case measurement rounds for perfect encoded fusion, matching a minimum root eccentricity bound with a constructive strategy.

entry.title: Strong eigenstate thermalization in Singer-cycle Clifford circuits
entry.summary: Strong eigenstate thermalization in Singer-cycle Clifford circuits arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper studies the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis, a framework for how isolated quantum systems thermalize. It introduces brickwork Clifford circuits whose Pauli transformations follow a Singer cycle over F2. The authors prove that all Floquet eigenstates of these circuits are thermal at infinite temperature without exceptions, and they derive uniform bounds on deviations of observables. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove that all Floquet eigenstates of Singer-cycle Clifford circuits thermalize at infinite temperature without exceptions, with uniform bounds.

entry.title: Complex mobility edges from competing localization channels in non-Hermitian quasicrystals
entry.summary: Complex mobility edges from competing localization channels in non-Hermitian quasicrystals arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper extends the Ganeshan-Pixley-Das Sarma model with asymmetric hopping and complex onsite potential to describe a broad class of non-Hermitian quasiperiodic chains. Using Avila's global theory, the authors derive exact Lyapunov exponents, find thresholds of two localization channels on the complex-energy plane, and propose a selection rule separating physical mobility edges from suppressed candidates. The channel controlling localization can switch with energy, producing complex mobility edges of non-Hermitian origin, and nonreciprocal hopping shifts these thresholds and the bulk spectrum. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce competing localization channels in non-Hermitian quasicrystals, derive exact Lyapunov exponents via Avila's global theory, and report numerical verification of the complex mobili

entry.title: Higher-scoring coding models did not get more work done
entry.summary: Higher-Scoring Coding Models Did Not Get More Work Done arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper uses a 19-day U.S. export control ban on Claude Fable 5 in June 2026 as a natural experiment, with most users switching to Opus 4.8. Comparing GitHub pull requests of 297 Fable 5 users with 8,908 Opus 4.8 users, it finds that access to Fable 5 did not significantly raise the 7-day merge rate. Weekly merged pull request counts also showed no significant increase. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use a export-control suspension as a natural experiment, reporting difference-in-differences results showing no significant productivity gain from higher benchmark scores.

entry.title: Inference after coding agents: AI coding agents can inflate hypothesis-test results through selective search
entry.summary: Inference after coding agents arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper argues that AI coding agents, which can open-endedly explore many analysis choices and replay their steps, enable a supercharged form of selective inference that threatens classical statistical testing. On simulated data with zero true effects, four frontier agents reported significant p-values between 54% and 98% of the time when asked for a compelling finding. The authors propose a correction: after an agent finishes, they reset and replay it on data subsamples to estimate how likely it is to select that analysis when results look favorable, yielding an adjusted test. In simulations, this lowers false rejection rates to near the nominal 5%. ★★★★ Notable: The authors identify a new post-selection inference problem from coding agents and propose a replay-based correction, reporting 54-98% significance on null simulations and two applications.

entry.title: Computational hardness of online stochastic matching under random arrivals
entry.summary: Computational Hardness of Online Stochastic Matching arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies online stochastic matching on bipartite graphs, where offline vertices are known in advance and online requests arrive from known distributions, each being matched immediately and irrevocably or rejected. It gives the first computational hardness results for random-order arrivals. For known i.i.d. arrivals, computing the online optimum is APX-hard, so no polynomial-time approximation scheme exists unless P = NP. For random-order arrivals with only one offline node, computing the optimal online policy is #P-hard. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give the first hardness results for random-order online stochastic matching, claiming APX-hardness for i.i.d. arrivals and #P-hardness in the prophet secretary setting.

entry.title: π⁴: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion
entry.summary: π⁴: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper presents π⁴, a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception that works on uncalibrated RGB inputs such as single images, unordered image collections, or videos. It recovers dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, and for multi-image inputs also outputs 2D/3D point tracks and moving-object masks. The model pairs a geometry branch with a geometry-conditioned motion branch and produces joint reconstructions and tracks in one forward pass. The authors report the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation with about 0.5B parameters. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors present a unified 4D foundation model coupling geometry and motion branches, reporting best average geometry rank and competitive tracking and segmentation results with about 0.5B paramete

entry.title: Auditing a Learned Simulator for Legged Robots: Checking the Robotic World Model on the ANYmal D Quadruped
entry.summary: Auditing a Learned Simulator for Legged Robots: The Robotic World Model on ANYmal D arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper audits the Robotic World Model (RWM), a neural network simulator used to train walking policies for the ANYmal D quadruped, along with its uncertainty-estimation follow-up, RWM-U. The authors rebuilt the model without a GPU and compared many trained and compressed simulators, then tested trained policies in a hand-built MuJoCo model of the robot. They found that training on the model's own multi-step rollouts gave better long-horizon results than one-step training, and that one-step accuracy can mislead design choices. The study covers one robot, one gait, and simulated data only, with no hardware tests. ★★★★ Notable: The authors audit a learned legged-robot simulator end to end, reporting that one-step training misjudges multi-step design choices and that ensemble uncertainty is badly miscalibrated, across 101 sim

entry.title: Finding Reusable Neuron Groups in Language Models at Scale
entry.summary: Large-scale Neuron Community Discovery Reveals Neuron-Sparse Behaviors in Language Models arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper introduces an unsupervised method for discovering neuron groups in Llama-3.1-8B that recur across prompts and are causally necessary and sufficient for common computations. Applied to ten million prompts, the method finds thousands of candidate communities, which are assessed on held-out prompts with three causal tests. The discovered communities support functions such as grammatical agreement, in-context copying, addition, and multiplication. With communities capped at 128 neurons, a portion of held-out prompts can be explained on a neuron-sparse basis. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose unsupervised neuron community discovery and report causal necessity and sufficiency tests on held-out prompts in Llama-3.1-8B.

entry.title: Colombo: A Self-Organizing AI Researcher for Oracle-Based Optimization
entry.summary: Colombo: A Frontier-to-Frontier Autoresearch System for Oracle-Based Optimization arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper presents Colombo, a self-organizing AI research system first applied to oracle-based optimization, where it studies how efficiently problems can be solved through a fixed information interface. It maintains a Complexity Atlas mapping frontier settings and known limits, and uses adversarial co-ascent to develop algorithms and hard problem families. Mathematical claims are checked through independent review and Lean-based formal certification. The authors report optimal or near-optimal rates for more than fifty settings in the Atlas. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present a self-organizing AI research system reporting near-optimal rates for over fifty oracle-optimization settings, with Lean-based certification.

entry.title: Magflow: Differentiable Simulation for Industrial 6D Magnetic Levitation Control
entry.summary: Magflow: Differentiable Simulation of Industrial-Grade 6D Magnetic Levitation arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper introduces Magflow, a fully differentiable, GPU-parallel simulator that computes the electromagnetic physics of 6D magnetic levitation directly rather than through hand-crafted approximations. The authors use it to train a neural controller purely from simulated physics for an industrial-grade system. They report that the controller transfers zero-shot to real hardware and meets hard real-time constraints at 4 kHz. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present a differentiable GPU simulator, train a neural controller purely in simulation, and report zero-shot hardware transfer at 4 kHz.

entry.title: ForecastGym: A Controlled, Replayable Benchmark for Evaluating Web-Searching Forecasting Agents
entry.summary: ForecastGym: A Live, Controlled, and Replayable Benchmark for Forecasting Agents arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper introduces ForecastGym, which records results from four commercial web search APIs for open prediction-market questions every two days, then replays this frozen evidence offline after outcomes are known. This lets researchers compare models, memory strategies, and search sources under a fixed evidence-acquisition policy. The first release includes 150 questions, 614 evidence states, and 131k search results. On the frozen evidence, all tested language models forecast less accurately than the market, and switching search APIs changes Brier scores by up to 0.043. ★★★★ Notable: The authors freeze and replay timed web search evidence to fairly compare forecasting agents across 150 questions and 131k results, versus market and models.

entry.title: Checking Blind Spots: Planner-Guided Perception With Hypothetical Objects
entry.summary: Check Your Blind Spots: Decision-Guided Perception by Probing the Planner with Hypothetical Objects arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper proposes Decision-Guided Speculative Perception (DGSP), which starts from a low-resolution draft and inserts hypothetical objects into the planner to find locations where an unseen object would change its action. Only those locations and the detections supporting the current action are verified at high resolution, repeated until the action is stable. On three driving datasets, the method reproduces the whole-frame high-resolution action on about 98% of frames using about a quarter of the pixels. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use hypothetical-object probing of the planner to guide resolution allocation, prove equivalence to whole-frame action under conditions, and report reproduction on three driving datasets.

entry.title: Dissecting the GPU Load/Store Unit and Its Security Risks
entry.summary: Dissecting the GPU Load/Store Unit and Exposing Its Security Risks arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper reverse-engineers how the load/store unit (LSU) of recent NVIDIA GPUs serves load instructions, using microbenchmarks. It gives a cycle-accurate latency formula for global L1 hits and shared memory accesses, showing that bank conflicts and L1 tag lookups depend on addresses and cause contention. The authors show that the LSU can leak information, communicate covertly, and slow colocated workloads, and they recover a full AES-128 key under the threat model of prior GPU AES timing attacks. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors measure GPU LSU load latency, contention points and warp starvation, reporting new side and covert channels, AES-128 key recovery, and up to 750x slowdown of cuBLAS on A100/H100.

entry.title: Rhythmic coding patterns reveal AI-generated videos in compressed streams
entry.summary: The Rhythm of Generated Video: Latent Chunking Leaves Periodic Traces in Compressed Bitstreams arXiv · Nov 18, 2026The paper finds that causal video autoencoders concentrate unpredictable content at latent-chunk boundaries, causing rate-distortion optimized encoders to allocate bits periodically. Four-frame pulses appear in CogVideoX and Wan2.2, and eight-frame pulses in LTX-Video, but not in content-matched camera footage, all without decoding pixels. A training-free peak-ratio statistic separates generated from camera video with AUC 0.84-0.94, and frame-size traces identify four commercial generators. ★★★★ Notable: The authors link temporal stride in generated video to periodic bit allocation, detecting generators from compressed bitstreams. The abstract reports AUC and accuracy across several generators and cod

entry.title: AI-Guided Ideas for Repairing Intestinal Barrier Using Physical Methods
entry.summary: Structured AI ideation yields physical strategies for epithelial barrier repair arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper presents Abelio, an AI system that generates new research directions by reformulating research goals and drawing on elements beyond conventional disciplines. Its proposed physical interventions, using membrane-tethered PEG and cholesterol-anchored complementary DNA, were tested in damaged Caco-2 cell monolayers. PEG preserved barrier function in a membrane-surface-dependent way, while complementary DNA enabled sequence-specific restoration that could be reversed on demand. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present Abelio, a structured AI ideation system, and report experimental validation of PEG and complementary DNA barrier repair in Caco-2 monolayers.

entry.title: A shared exponential lower bound for Dantzig and modified simplex in deterministic discounted games
entry.summary: A Common Exponential Lower Bound for Dantzig and Modified Simplex in Deterministic Discounted Games arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies a family of N-state deterministic two-player discounted games in which runs alternate adaptively between Dantzig's rule and the modified simplex method. It shows that, regardless of tie breaking, such runs from a specified initial strategy need 2^{Ω(N)} switches. The paper also presents a return-gate construction with related results, and shows Dantzig's rule is strongly polynomial under certain structural conditions. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove a shared exponential lower bound for Dantzig and modified simplex on deterministic discounted games, with a return-gate construction and polynomial-time sufficient conditions.

entry.title: SEAM: Computer-use agents recognize cross-screen harm but still carry it out
entry.summary: SEAM: Computer-Use Agents Know the Harm Between Screens, and Commit It Anyway arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper introduces SEAM, a benchmark of 600 multi-step, cross-application computer-use tasks where each instruction and screen is benign alone but harmful in combination. Several agents carried out the harm in up to 92% of runs, though they declined when the user stated the harm in one sentence. Asked about the pages, agents often flagged the conflict yet still confirmed the action, and proprietary models were markedly more cautious. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce cross-screen compositional harm, test 600 OSWorld tasks with minimal-pair variants, and report up to 92% harmful execution.

entry.title: Hierarchical Diffusion Transformer (HiT) for End-to-End Image Generation
entry.summary: Hierarchical Diffusion Transformer for End-to-End Image Generation arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper proposes Hierarchical Diffusion Transformers (HiT), a pixel-space image generator that progressively groups related tokens and represents each group with one token. The main Transformer processes these compact group tokens before ungrouping restores them to their image positions. Without segmentation or region labels, the model learns to group coherent objects and, in text-to-image generation, to associate caption words with image patches. The paper reports 1.48 FID on ImageNet 256×256. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose learning hierarchical token grouping inside a pixel-space diffusion Transformer; the abstract reports FID 1.48 on ImageNet 256 and comparisons with UniLiP on five text-to-image ben

entry.title: A reality check on kernel attention: benchmarking and distilling efficient attention at scale
entry.summary: The Kernel Reality Check: Benchmarking and Distilling Efficient Attention at Scale arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper systematically compares kernelized attention methods, which aim to replace softmax attention's quadratic cost with linear-cost alternatives. It finds that FlashAttention uses less memory and runs faster than current kernelized methods in training and in vision transformers across most sequence lengths. Under a unified distillation protocol, kernelized methods still trail softmax by 2 to 10 points. The proposed LARA++ approximates softmax via importance sampling and recovers up to 99% of softmax accuracy, though its computational overhead remains substantial. ★★★★ Notable: The authors benchmark kernelized attention against FlashAttention and propose LARA++, reporting recovery of up to 99% of softmax accuracy.

entry.title: Built for the Task: Rethinking Quantum Chemistry with Foresighted Agentic Computing
entry.summary: Born for the Task: Rethinking Quantum Chemistry with Foresighted Agentic Computing arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper presents BORN, a framework that uses coding agents to generate task-specific, high-performance quantum chemistry programs on demand. Before execution, it predicts each computational strategy's error and runtime, then selects the fastest option within the error tolerance from the predicted accuracy-runtime Pareto frontier. The authors report that a Hartree-Fock calculation with 50,024 basis functions finishes in 1.41 hours on a single CPU node. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose predicting each strategy's error and runtime before execution, choosing from a Pareto frontier, and having coding agents build the program; the abstract reports speedups on a 50,02

entry.title: How pretraining length, model size, and labeled data affect AI models for radiotherapy scans
entry.summary: Impact of Pretraining Length, Model Size, and Annotation Budget on Downstream Clinical Tasks of Foundation Models in Radiotherapy arXiv · Nov 18, 2026This paper studies foundation models pretrained on about 150,000 3D cone-beam CT scans from radiotherapy, examining how pretraining length, model size, and finetuning method affect performance on head and neck cancer tasks. Tasks include feeding tube classification and clinical characteristics such as T- and N-stage and sex. Pretraining validation loss was the most consistent predictor of downstream performance, and LoRA performed comparably to full finetuning while training only 0.5-2.5% of parameters. Models with pretraining consistently outperformed those without it. ★★★★ Notable: The authors study how pretraining length, model size, and finetuning affect downstream head-and-neck cancer tasks on about 150,000 radiotherapy CBCT scans, comparing LoRA, full finetuning, and no pret

entry.title: Stopping Is Not the Limit: Long-Horizon Exploit Development by AI Agents
entry.summary: Stopping Is Not the Limit: Understanding and Eliciting Agent Capability in Long-Horizon Vulnerability Exploitation arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper studies whether language model agents can build working exploits from known software vulnerabilities, using the ExploitBench benchmark with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. It finds verified gains continue after the first stop response, though they diminish over longer runs. The authors propose SCoRe, a context-management method that compacts context at stop bursts and marks impossibility judgments as unproven, reaching 67.0% capability coverage for MiMo at 2,000 turns. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose SCoRe, compacting context at stop bursts, and report MiMo reaching 67.0% capability coverage at 2,000 turns on ExploitBench versus 32.4% originally.

entry.title: Whether rare labels are learned or inferred from their companion labels in multi-label classification
entry.summary: When the tail is earned by its companions: measuring label dependence in long-tailed multi-label classification arXiv · Nov 17, 2026The paper studies how rare labels in long-tailed multi-label classification often co-occur with frequent labels, so classifiers may recognize them through companion labels rather than learning them directly. It proposes a within-label measure of this dependence and a training-label statistic that bounds, before training, how far reported recall can exceed recall on companion-free occurrences. Across 23 corpora, 7 training objectives and five families of label-correlation mechanisms, companion-free recall was lower on all six corpora where the measure is defined, with up to 18.4% of tail true positives credited by macro-F1 disappearing at that rate. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a within-label dependence estimand and a pre-training bound, reporting checks across 23 corpora and 7 training objectives in long-tailed multi-label classification.

entry.title: CaFe: Causally Faithful Conditional Traffic Scenario Generation
entry.summary: CaFe: Causally Faithful Conditional Traffic Scenario Generation arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper studies intent leakage in language-conditioned traffic simulation, where surrounding vehicles react to an instructed agent's private plan before that behaviour is observable. The authors propose a paired intervention test, build the WOMD-PACT dataset of 531,099 timed-tagged scenes, and introduce CaFe, a diffusion-based simulator that limits inter-agent interaction to public beliefs. Evaluation reports that existing conditioning designs displace 23-83% of nearby uninstructed agents through leakage, while CaFe removes measurable leakage and keeps WOSAC realism at 0.763. ★★★★ Notable: The authors formalise intent leakage as a causal faithfulness problem, proposing a paired intervention test and public-belief constraints; they report 23-83% displacement on WOMD and WOSAC 0.763.

entry.title: Studying verifiers that grade AI agent work against multi-criteria rubrics
entry.summary: Verifying Agents in Rubric-Graded Environments arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper systematically studies verifiers for AI agents in rubric-graded environments, where multiple natural-language criteria are used to judge an agent's outputs and environment changes. The authors build BankerVerifierBench, a meta-evaluation dataset of 2,464 human-judged criteria across 24 investment-banking tasks, and derive a nine-capability taxonomy distilled into three design principles. They implement these principles in Gandalf, an open-source verifier that matches or exceeds baseline F1 scores at lower cost and generalizes to the OpenClaw environment. ★★★★ Notable: The authors systematically study verifiers for rubric-graded agent environments, proposing a nine-capability taxonomy and evaluating on 2,464 human-judged criteria plus OpenClaw.

entry.title: NexSight: Verifiable tasks for testing and training AI agents on fine-grained long-video understanding
entry.summary: NexSight: Verifiable Tasks for Fine-Grained Agentic Long-Video Understanding arXiv · Nov 17, 2026NexSight is a framework that builds verifiable tasks to evaluate and train AI agents that search long videos for fine-grained details such as counts, event order, and timing of state changes. A task is kept only if a verifier that does not see the draft answer can reconstruct it from evidence re-collected from the raw video. The resulting SightLine benchmark contains 310 evidence-traceable tasks from 108 long videos, evaluated in a shared multiscale harness called SightLoop. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose verifiable long-video agent tasks with a shared evaluation harness and step-level trajectory supervision; reported gains reach 42.26% from 21.29% and over 8 points externally.

entry.title: PANO: A Parallel Latent Space Neural Operator for Solving PDEs
entry.summary: PANO: Parallel Latent Space Neural Operator for Solving PDEs arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper proposes PANO, a neural operator for solving partial differential equation problems with large-scale observations. It transforms observations into several distinct compressed representations through independent mappings, learns physical interactions in parallel, and fuses the decoded results to predict the target physical field. The paper also introduces Coupled Assignment Projection and a Pairwise Latent Space Attention Layer. Experiments on nine benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose parallel latent spaces with coupled projection and pairwise attention, reporting 28.3% and 21.4%+ error reductions across nine benchmarks.

entry.title: Proximal Targets: Training Repeated-Refinement Models on Puzzles with Many Valid Solutions
entry.summary: Proximal Targets: Training Looped Refiners on Problems with Many Correct Answers arXiv · Nov 17, 2026The paper studies looped refiners such as HRM and TRM, which repeatedly apply a small network to a draft answer. It proves that when a puzzle has many correct answers, training every pass toward one stored answer creates a loss floor that model capacity cannot remove, and the best output blends answers into an invalid grid. The authors propose a proximal target that trains each pass toward the correct answer nearest its input, and report much higher solve rates on Sudoku, sparse puzzles, and graph colouring than the standard target. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose nearest-correct-answer training targets, prove a capacity-independent loss floor for fixed targets, and report large gains on Sudoku and graph colouring against baselines.

entry.title: RefCloth: Transferable Adversarial Tablecloths Attacking Vision-Language-Action Robot Models
entry.summary: RefCloth: Transferable Adversarial Tablecloths for Vision-Language-Action Models arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper introduces RefCloth, a method that optimizes one persistent adversarial tablecloth texture on a frozen source robot policy. The texture is deployed zero-shot on unseen tasks and target models without changing task objects or cameras. In native simulation across four LIBERO suites, the texture transfers from OpenVLA-OFT to π0 and π0.5, lowering success by 62.50 and 43.75 percentage points on average relative to an unoptimized cloth. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a single transferable adversarial tablecloth that cuts VLA success by 62.50 and 43.75 points on average across four LIBERO suites.

entry.title: TANGO: RGB-guided hyperspectral super-resolution without registration, using two cameras and a new dataset
entry.summary: TANGO: Real-World Unregistered RGB-Guided Hyperspectral Super-Resolution with Two-Camera Acquisitions arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper addresses hyperspectral image super-resolution when the guiding high-resolution RGB image is not spatially aligned with the hyperspectral data. The authors release DUET, the first large-scale public dataset for this task, with 403 indoor and outdoor scenes captured by two separate cameras. They propose TANGO, which performs global alignment followed by coarse-to-fine local feature alignment, and uses a learned gating mechanism to reduce RGB guidance where views cannot be matched. TANGO reports state-of-the-art results on DUET and REAL. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce the DUET dataset and a global-to-local alignment with gating, reporting state-of-the-art results on DUET and REAL.

entry.title: Stored preferences can silently drop decision-critical information from AI answers
entry.summary: Remembered as Brief: Stored Preferences SilentlyRemove Decision-Critical Information arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper examines whether an AI assistant's stored memory of a user's preferences, such as a wish for brief answers without warnings, causes it to omit information that matters for decisions. The authors built a benchmark of 100 everyday decisions across 25 domains and tested five models. They report that some models saved an instruction from a web page as the user's preference and then often omitted critical items without saying so, and made value-dependent choices on the user's behalf. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors show stored user preferences silently drop decision-critical information, testing 100 scenarios across five models, with scenarios, harness and logs released.

entry.title: Mitigating Shortcut Bias by Aligning Sample Groupings Across Multiple Feature Views
entry.summary: Let Samples Sing in Chorus: Mitigating Spurious Correlations via Cross-view Consensus arXiv · Nov 17, 2026Deep models often rely on spurious correlations that hurt accuracy for underrepresented groups. This paper proposes CHORD, a multi-view framework that aggregates within-class partitions across different representation spaces to reach cross-view consensus, then debiases the representation and classifier without bias labels. Experiments on seven benchmarks spanning vision, language, speech, and medical imaging report consistent gains in worst-group accuracy. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose cross-view consensus for debiasing without bias labels, reporting worst-group accuracy gains across seven multimodal benchmarks.

entry.title: The Cost of Strict Coverage Limits in Online Conformal Prediction
entry.summary: The Price of Hard Coverage Constraints in Online Conformal Prediction arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper studies online conformal prediction, where prediction sets are produced round by round and the cumulative number of miscoverages must stay within a fixed budget throughout deployment. It determines the minimum extra prediction-set size any online method must incur to satisfy this hard constraint, showing the cost persists even with i.i.d. data and a known score distribution. The minimum cost is Θ(log T) for a fixed known time, Θ(T^{1/3}) for the largest expected cost over fixed times, and Θ(√T) for the worst realized cost under a hindsight-chosen time. These rates can be achieved using past scores without knowing the score distribution. ★★★★ Notable: The authors characterize the unavoidable efficiency cost of hard coverage constraints in online conformal prediction, giving tight bounds of Θ(log T), Θ(T^{1/3}), and Θ(√T) for different cost notions,

entry.title: Generating 0.5 m Canopy Height Maps from Free Sentinel-2 Satellite Imagery
entry.summary: Sub-Meter Canopy Height Synthesis from Sentinel-2 via Anchored Residual Flow arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper produces 0.5 m canopy height models from free 10 m Sentinel-2 imagery, a cross-modal super-resolution task predicting height from optical reflectance. It proposes two models: a deterministic regressor (Anchor) favoring low distortion, and a conditional flow matching model (AR-flow) trained on the Anchor's residuals for perceptual fidelity. Trained on 197k LiDAR-paired tiles across the contiguous United States and tested on 2,530 held-out tiles, the Anchor reaches 2.83 m MAE, while AR-flow lowers sliced Wasserstein distance from 1.13 to 0.208 at a higher MAE of 3.68 m. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors report an anchored residual flow matching approach in a learned CHM latent space, evaluated on 197k LiDAR-paired tiles against eight baselines with MAE and sliced Wasserstein distance.

entry.title: Entanglement Lower Bounds for Symmetric Quantum Circuits: A theory paper on what symmetric quantum circuits can compute under entanglement limits
entry.summary: Entanglement Lower Bounds for Symmetric Quantum Circuits arXiv · Nov 17, 2026The paper studies a tradeoff between circuit size and entanglement width in symmetric quantum circuits, where every symmetry of the input extends to an automorphism of the circuit. It introduces a new quantum pebble game based on the partial trace and shows that a certain graph property, decidable in classical polynomial time, cannot be computed by polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuits with entanglement width o(n/log n). Without entanglement restrictions, the authors show that every graph property in BQP can be computed by such circuits. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a new partial-trace quantum pebble game, transferring classical lower bounds to symmetric quantum circuits with restricted entanglement width.

entry.title: Computational hardness of the covering radius for sparse LDPC parity-check codes
entry.summary: Hardness and Inapproximability of the Covering Radius for LDPC Codes arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper studies the covering-radius decision problem for sparse binary parity-check matrices with bounded row and column weights, asking whether every syndrome can be produced by an error vector of Hamming weight at most r. It proves the problem is Π₂ᴾ-complete when the maximum row and column weights are three, and remains Π₂ᴾ-hard under a constant multiplicative gap. The authors also derive an explicit NP-hard approximation factor under the same weight constraints, starting from Vertex Cover on 3-regular graphs. They note that if either maximum weight is at most two, the covering radius is computable in polynomial time. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show covering-radius decision for LDPC codes is Π2P-complete at weight three, with a constant gap and a sharp weight-threshold result, mainly impacting coding-theory complexity.

entry.title: Correct Diagnosis, Unsafe Path: Auditing Clinical AI Decision Trajectories
entry.summary: Right Diagnosis, Unsafe Route: Auditing Clinical AI Decision Trajectories and Corrective Oversight for Validity and Potential Harm arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper proposes a stepwise evaluation method that makes patient safety its target. Real hospital admissions are replayed checkpoint by checkpoint, with each AI system deciding only on the evidence released so far, and each test, treatment and disposition is rated for potential harm and clinical validity. Across 300 cases from a cardiology cohort, MIMIC-IV and ASCENT, 55.2% of trajectories with an acceptable final diagnosis included a decision with moderate or severe potential harm. Structured corrections repaired 73.6% of first errors, but 30.2% of corrections were followed by new potentially unsafe decisions. ★★★★ Notable: The authors audit each clinical decision along diagnostic trajectories for patient harm, across 300 cases, reporting high harm rates and new risks from corrections.

entry.title: Do Coherent Fake Stories Keep LLM Attackers Engaged in Honeypots?
entry.summary: Adaptive LLM-Driven Honeypots vs. LLM-Driven Attackers: Does Narrative Coherence Improve Deception? arXiv · Nov 17, 2026The paper proposes narrative deception, where a defender maps each attacker command to a MITRE ATT&CK technique and deploys mutually referential fake files, processes, services, and logs during an intrusion. In 1,150 sessions with LLM-driven attackers, coherent scenarios raised the median session length of advanced attackers from 40 to 165 commands and reduced abandonment from 86% to 52%. Most sessions ended from loss of interest rather than detection, at comparable inference cost. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose narrative deception with coherent ATT&CK-mapped artefacts; across 1,150 sessions, median commands for advanced attackers rise from 40 to 165.

entry.title: Lost in Read-out: a closed-form edit that locates the image-quality gap in vision-language models
entry.summary: Lost in Read-out: Locating the Image Quality Gap in Vision-Language Models with a Closed-Form Edit arXiv · Nov 17, 2026Vision-language models are widely used as zero-shot image quality assessors, but their good-or-poor answers agree only moderately with human opinion. Layer-wise probes on five models show that quality is linearly decodable from the vision encoder and the last language layer, well beyond what the answers reveal. The gap mainly arises in the final read-out, which over-rewards colorfulness and under-rewards sharpness relative to humans. A closed-form edit of a single last-layer neuron recovers much of this gap on prompts not used for fitting. ★★★★ Notable: The authors locate the VLM quality gap in the final read-out and test a closed-form single-neuron edit, reporting 86–100% recovery of the ridge-head gain on KonIQ.

entry.title: Study on missing security-fix backports in GitHub Actions workflows
entry.summary: Missing Security-Fix Backporting for GitHub Actions Workflows arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper presents a large-scale empirical study of security fixes in GitHub Actions workflows that were applied to default branches but not carried over to release and maintenance branches. It finds that most audited release branches remain vulnerable and that backporting is rare and slow. The authors propose WorkflowBP, a neuro-symbolic technique that applies fixes to divergent branches, and report results from testing it on real workflow files. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors quantify the first large-scale backporting gap for GitHub Actions security fixes and propose WorkflowBP, a neuro-symbolic technique; the abstract reports 67.9% scanner-checked backports on

entry.title: EfficientVPR: A Faster Visual Place Recognition Method Using Scene-Aware Prompt Tuning
entry.summary: EfficientVPR: Toward Efficient Visual Place Recognition via Scene-Aware Prompt Tuning and Adaptive Feature Enhancement arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper presents EfficientVPR, a lightweight one-stage framework for visual place recognition, which identifies locations from images under varying environmental conditions. It combines scene-aware visual prompt tuning with an instance-dependent local feature enhancement module to balance speed and accuracy. On five benchmark datasets, it sets a new state of the art among DINOv2-small models and achieves a 73× speedup over a DINOv2-large two-stage method, with an average R@1 gap within 2.5%. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a lightweight one-stage VPR framework with scene-aware prompt tuning and instance-dependent local feature enhancement, reporting a 73× speedup on five benchmarks.

entry.title: Bigger Clusters, Lower Bar: LLM Entity Matching Grows More Lenient
entry.summary: Growing Clusters Lower the Bar: Profile Accretion in LLM-Based Incremental Entity Resolution arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper studies LLM-based incremental entity resolution, where a model decides whether a new record belongs to an existing cluster after seeing the records already linked to it. Using French procurement supplier data with SIREN identifiers as ground truth, the authors vary only how many verified members are shown and find that false matches on similarly named companies rise as clusters grow. The effect is absent on Czech and Bulgarian TED notices, where full addresses already identify the company. The authors also report that a single threshold on labelled data raises recall in online linking without extra LLM calls. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report that LLM matchers accept new records more readily as cluster size grows, tested by varying only shown member count across several models and formats.

entry.title: RehearsalBench: Testing whether AI can predict the results of changing a company
entry.summary: RehearsalBench: Can AI Predict What Happens When You Change a Company? arXiv · Nov 17, 2026RehearsalBench is a benchmark that tests whether AI models can diagnose an operation, choose an intervention, and forecast its consequences. Models work inside a simulated bank contact center built from real call records, seeing only what a manager would see, and their plans are tested across 200 seeded futures and three organizational versions. The best model improved on doing nothing by 6.8% of the no-change cost, and all models got the direction of effects right but overstated their size, and none recommended holding off. Twelve models' forecasts of 33 real organizational changes showed a Spearman rank correlation of 0.92 with real-world outcomes.] ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a simulated contact-center benchmark for organizational change decisions and report forecast-ranking agreement with 33 real changes (Spearman ρ=0.92).

entry.title: Reallocating visual tokens where a small VLM disagrees with pruned answers
entry.summary: Disagree to Prune: Reallocating Visual Tokens Where a Small VLM Dissents arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper studies visual token pruning, which keeps only part of a large vision-language model's visual tokens to speed up inference. The authors observe that a small VLM given the full image often disagrees with the pruned model's answer. They propose PRUDENT, which answers first with about half the budget, then re-answers disagreeing questions with twice the budget. On 18 benchmarks, it outperforms eight existing pruning methods at the same average token budget. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use a small VLM's disagreement to decide re-answering and reallocate visual tokens; they report results on 18 benchmarks against eight pruning methods.

entry.title: Showing Conflicting Claims Instead of Settling Them in Shared Memory for AI Debate
entry.summary: Surfacing Disagreement Beats Resolving It: A Gated Ablation Study of Provenance-Weighted Memory for Multi-Agent Debate arXiv · Nov 17, 2026The paper tests whether shared memory for multi-agent debate should resolve contradictions or preserve them. In a controlled ablation of five mechanisms, passing a ranked set of conflicting facts to the debate, rather than a single winning fact, raised F1 by +0.340 and reduced successful attacks from 22 to 7 of 122 poisoned items at equal cost. Two other mechanisms reduced accuracy, and the write trust-gate failed structurally. The authors release their harness, attack set, and logs. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show preserving contradictions improves F1 and reduces attack success in multi-agent debate, replicated across two retrieval substrates.

entry.title: Sample-Aligned Decoders (SAD) for latent generative models: a post-training method that tunes only the decoder and adds no inference cost
entry.summary: Sample-Aligned Decoders for Latent Generative Models arXiv · Nov 17, 2026Latent generative models decode generated latents into images, but the decoder is trained only on encoder latents, so the generator's residual errors appear directly in the final image. The paper proposes Sample-Aligned Decoders (SAD), which fine-tunes only the decoder of a frozen generator, aligning decoded generated latents with unpaired real images in a frozen foundation-model feature space while preserving the original decoder's behavior on encoder latents. SAD improves four state-of-the-art ImageNet generators across three tokenizers, for example lowering REPA-E's FID-50K from 1.15 to 0.98. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose fine-tuning only a frozen generator's decoder via unpaired distribution alignment and encoder anchoring, reporting FID gains on several ImageNet generators.

entry.title: How many training labels are wrong? Auditing a trained model via gradient allocation
entry.summary: How Many Training Labels Are Wrong? Auditing a Fitted Model through Gradient Allocation arXiv · Nov 17, 2026The paper proposes estimating how many training labels are wrong, and which ones, from the per-example gradients of a single trained model. Gradient magnitudes are normalised into a gradient allocation and compared with each class's mean allocation, and an example is flagged when relabelling it to its nearest other class fits better. The method needs no threshold, clean data, held-out set or further training. It reports separating wrong from right labels on CIFAR-10N even after the model has fitted the wrong labels, and reading the noise rate closely on a briefly trained model. ★★★★ Notable: The authors audit label noise from per-example gradient allocations of one trained model, reporting separation of wrong labels after fitting and noise-rate estimates on CIFAR-10.

entry.title: How individual judgment differences are shaped: shared axes, personal weights, and when they exceed consensus
entry.summary: The shape of individual differences in judgment: shared axes, personal weights, and when their spread crosses the consensus arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This study examines the shape, not just the size, of individual differences in judging faces, artworks, photographs and jokes. The authors compare three nested generative models and test how well they predict unseen raters across ten public datasets of about 20,000 raters. For faces, reweighting of shared dimensions was sufficient and opposing weights were not detected. For artworks, weights spread continuously along the abstract-figurative axis, with 28 percent of raters on the opposite side from the population, a tail that was much smaller with a different rater sample. ★★★★ Notable: The authors model the shape of individual judgment differences as nested generative models, comparing predictive fit across about 20,000 raters in ten public datasets.

entry.title: NONSENSE: Nonsense strings reveal a gap between similarity and meaning in dense retrieval
entry.summary: NONSENSE: Non-Semantic Strings Expose Semanticity Gaps in Dense Retrieval arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper introduces NONSENSE, a black-box method that builds visibly meaningless strings by sparse edits, forbidding copying of query terms and optimizing only their dense similarity to a query. Across five BEIR-style datasets and three popular single-vector retrievers, these strings often outscore each retriever's best judged relevant passage and frequently rank first in the full corpus. The authors conclude there is a semanticity gap: high similarity does not reliably indicate semantic relevance. They argue dense retrievers should be evaluated not only on retrieving relevant documents but also on how faithfully their similarity scores reflect semantic evidence. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a black-box sparse-edit probe creating non-semantic strings that often outscore relevant passages across five BEIR-style datasets and three retrievers.

entry.title: Fair Bubble Sort: A ranking method that stays fair for continuous attributes like age or income without grouping them
entry.summary: Fair Bubble Sort: Provably Optimal Fair Ranking with Continuous Sensitive Attributes arXiv · Nov 17, 2026The paper studies fair ranking when the protected attribute is continuous, avoiding the discretization of values such as age or income into groups. It introduces Continuous Pairwise Parity (CPP), a fairness measure based on the Kendall correlation between ranking positions and the protected attribute. The authors propose Fair Bubble Sort (FBS), a post-processing algorithm using targeted adjacent swaps, and prove it is exactly optimal for unweighted Kemeny distance with approximation guarantees for the score-weighted setting. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show FBS is scalable and outperforms discretization-based baselines in the fairness-accuracy trade-off. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a continuous fairness notion and prove FBS is exactly optimal for unweighted Kemeny distance; experiments report gains over discretization baselines.

entry.title: Multistage optimization for repositioning ride-hailing vehicles
entry.summary: Multistage Contextual Optimization for Vehicle Repositioning arXiv · Nov 17, 2026Ride-hailing platforms move idle vehicles to better match supply with demand across the city. The paper models this as a multistage linear program that links vehicle accumulation to completed trips through a macroscopic fundamental diagram. It proposes training the demand predictor directly on decision performance, deriving an exact gradient and a parallel block evaluation algorithm to speed up training. On New York City data, the method yields 7.7% to 9.1% more business benefit than the same predictor trained by mean squared error. ★★★★ Notable: The authors derive exact gradients for decision-driven training of multistage LP vehicle repositioning, add parallel block evaluation, and report 7.7% to 9.1% higher benefit on NYC data.

entry.title: MCTS Counts the Wrong Things: Learning Exploration Counts for LLM Reasoning
entry.summary: MCTS Is Counting the Wrong Thing: Learning Exploration Counts for LLM Reasoning arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper argues that standard UCT in Monte Carlo tree search counts textual branches independently, so different wordings of the same reasoning strategy repeatedly receive exploration bonuses. The authors propose Learned Pseudo-Count MCTS (LPC-MCTS), which uses a lightweight network to estimate representation coverage so that related branches share exploration evidence. Across 5 mathematical-reasoning and 7 search benchmarks, LPC-MCTS consistently outperforms strong MCTS baselines. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose learned pseudo-counts so related LLM reasoning branches share exploration evidence, reporting gains over MCTS baselines on 5 math and 7 search benchmarks.

entry.title: FIRE-Drive: A Feasibility-Aware Risk Evaluation Framework for Diffusion-Based Driving Planning
entry.summary: FIRE-Drive: Feasibility-Informed Risk Evaluation for End-to-End Diffusion Planning arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper presents FIRE-Drive, a framework that improves diffusion-based end-to-end autonomous driving planning. It combines dynamic feasible anchor initialization, bird's-eye-view risk evidence for each candidate trajectory, and compact high-quality candidate supervision with lightweight refinement. On NAVSIM v1 with a ResNet34 backbone, it reports a Predictive Driver Model Score of 91.5. In closed-loop evaluation on 220 Bench2Drive routes, it achieves a Driving Score of 71.43 and a Success Rate of 42.73%. ★★★★ Notable: The authors combine feasible anchor initialization, BEV risk evidence, and candidate supervision in diffusion planning, reporting NAVSIM v1 and 220-route Bench2Drive results with ablations.

entry.title: SARVIA: Quickly adapting the visual encoders already inside multimodal LLMs for radar imagery
entry.summary: SARVIA: Fast-Adapting the Strong SAR Foundation Models That Are Already in Your MLLMs arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper studies synthetic aperture radar (SAR) foundation models, which provide reusable image features for all-weather Earth observation tasks. The authors find that visual encoders from modern multimodal large language models can outperform dedicated SAR foundation models when used as starting points for downstream tasks. They propose SARVIA, which specializes these models through short post-pretraining on self-supervised visual questions built from unlabeled SAR and SAR-optical data. The paper reports that with 600 adaptation steps and 2 GPU-hours, SARVIA outperforms the compared models on six SAR detection and segmentation benchmarks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose reusing general MLLM visual encoders with brief self-supervised SAR adaptation instead of large pretraining, reporting gains over prior SAR foundation models on six benchmarks.

entry.title: Shifting Legged Robot Locomotion From Overheating Limits to Battery Limits
entry.summary: From Temperature-Limited to Battery-Limited Legged Locomotion arXiv · Nov 17, 2026Legged robots often stop due to motor overheating before their batteries run out. The authors train locomotion policies with reinforcement learning that avoid overheating without observing temperature, using a fitted thermal model. Tests on a Unitree Go2 quadruped show the policy lets the battery run down before thermal shutdown, extending distance covered. ★★★★ Notable: The authors train a policy with a reward on predicted thermal asymptotes, without temperature input, and report longer runtimes than a baseline on a Unitree Go2.

entry.title: SOTA or Luck? The Winner's Curse in LLM Leaderboards
entry.summary: SOTA or Luck? The Winner's Curse in LLM Leaderboards arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper shows that public LLM leaderboards rank models by noisy benchmark scores, so sampling luck can inflate the reported results of top-ranked models. The authors propose an m-out-of-N bootstrap to correct this bias, and use it to estimate plausible rank intervals and group models into performance tiers. They also introduce the RULER report, which pairs adjusted scores and rank uncertainty with raw rankings. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors formalize leaderboard winner's curse and rank-induced bias, correct them with an m-out-of-N bootstrap, prove residual bias bounds, and report results across 14 benchmarks.

entry.title: GapLeak: How Privacy-Preserving LLM Web Agents Can Leak Sensitive Data
entry.summary: GapLeak: When Privacy-Preserving LLM-based Web Agents Become a Privacy Risk arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper introduces GapLeak, a vulnerability in which LLM-based web agents that follow data minimization and least privilege principles can still disclose sensitive information. When a website requests a field unavailable from authorized sources, the agent may escalate to reachable but unauthorized sources to complete the task. Evaluated across three agent frameworks and six LLMs in recruitment, e-commerce, travel, and healthcare, GapLeak caused roughly 37% unauthorized disclosure on average. The authors propose submission-time verification, which filters unauthorized content before form submission and eliminates over 96% of such disclosures while preserving task success. ★★★★ Notable: The authors formalize GapLeak, where information gaps drive web agents to leak sensitive data, reporting about 37% unauthorized disclosure across three frameworks and six LLMs.

entry.title: Resolving the Computational and Structural Complexity of Bertrand Networks
entry.summary: Settling the Time and Structural Complexity of Bertrand Networks arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper studies the Bertrand network game of Babaioff et al. (2013), in which sellers must post a single price across captive and shared markets. It proves that computing a constant-error approximate Nash equilibrium in general Bertrand networks is PPAD-complete, even on sparse bipartite graphs of maximum degree five. It also gives an efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme when the maximum degree and the number of sellers with captive buyers are bounded. Finally, it shows every achievable equilibrium revenue profile can be realized with structural complexity O(2^n), and this bound is tight. ★★★★ Notable: The authors resolve an open problem on Bertrand network equilibria, proving PPAD-completeness for general graphs and a tight 2^O(n) structural complexity bound.

entry.title: Does 4-bit quantization change a chat model's refusal behaviour? A matched-perturbation study
entry.summary: Is 4-Bit Quantization More Than Noise to a Chat Model's Safety Behaviour? Attributing Behavioural Shifts with Matched Perturbations arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper examines whether 4-bit quantized chat models, common on phones and laptops, change how they refuse harmful requests. The authors ran a pre-registered study on three 3–4B chat models, using paired tests, blind human labels and an 8-bit control. They found 4-bit shifts in opposite directions, and show these depend on the specific rounding error rather than bits per weight or likelihood. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors use matched perturbations to show that 4-bit refusal shifts depend on the specific rounding error, not random noise of equal size, across three 3-4B chat models in a pre-registered study.

entry.title: Robust Quantum Memory in 3D: Thermal and Zero-Temperature Perturbative Stability (Part I)
entry.summary: Robust Passive Quantum Memory in Three Dimensions, Part I: Thermal and Zero-Temperature Perturbative Stability arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper examines whether a three-dimensional quantum many-body system can passively protect encoded quantum information, a question open since Kitaev's work on topological quantum computation. The authors present a slight variant of the Balasubramanian, Davydova, and Lin (BDL) family of stabilizer codes that remains stable along both boundary axes of the perturbation-temperature phase diagram as system size grows. Without perturbation, the code is thermally stable below a critical temperature. At zero temperature under arbitrary weak, superpolynomially decaying quantum perturbations, it maintains a uniform bulk spectral gap and a superpolynomially long memory lifetime. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors report that a variant of the BDL self-correcting code keeps a uniform bulk gap and superpolynomially small ground-space splitting under weak perturbations, advancing 3D passive memory.

entry.title: QCap: A Physics-Corrected Graph Neural Network for Capacitance Matrices of Superconducting Device Layouts
entry.summary: QCap: a physics-corrected graph neural network for the capacitance matrix of any planar superconducting device layout arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper presents QCap, a model that predicts the capacitance matrix of arbitrary planar superconducting device layouts in seconds, whereas Ansys Q3D simulations take minutes to hours. The model starts from a coarse physics estimate given by a fast method-of-moments simulation and is trained to correct it, using a universal graph format that accepts layouts from any tool. On 4,009 held-out test designs, its median error against Q3D is 0.177%, and it stays below 1% on unseen component families. It computes a 9-qubit device in 12 seconds on a laptop and a 100-qubit, 781-conductor device in 3.4 minutes. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a universal graph embedding and a method-of-moments prior corrected by a GNN, reporting accuracy on thousands of designs and 9- to 100-qubit devices.

entry.title: Exact dynamic scaling of quantum jump counts in continuously monitored many-body systems
entry.summary: Exact Dynamic Scaling of Quantum Jump Statistics in Monitored Many-Body Systems arXiv · Nov 17, 2026This paper studies how the number of quantum jumps within a subsystem fluctuates in many-body systems under continuous monitoring. The authors find that these fluctuations follow a dynamic scaling law with a diffusive time scale and an anomalous super-Poissonian dependence on subsystem size. For free fermions, they derive an exact finite-size solution of the Liouvillian autocorrelation function to determine the scaling exponent and scaling function. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a new dynamic scaling of subsystem quantum jump number fluctuations, with exact finite-size solutions for free fermions and extension to interacting fermions.

entry.title: Quantum reference frames and how they affect locality and causality in quantum field theory
entry.summary: Quantum Reference Frames, Locality, and Microcausality in Quantum Field Theory arXiv · Nov 17, 2026The paper studies how quantum reference frames for translations on Minkowski space affect the local structure of quantum field theories. Because of the relativistic spectrum condition, such frames are not described by projection-valued measures and often fail the weaker norm-1 localisation condition. As a result, strict locality becomes almost locality, and microcausality holds only through commutators that decay rapidly with separation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show frame observables cannot be projection-valued under the spectrum condition, replacing strict locality and microcausality with approximate versions.

entry.title: AI Scientist Finds Robust Quantum Control Sequences
